document: WHO recommendations on care for women with diabetes during pregnancy
quote: For pregnant women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, measure HbA1c in the first trimester or as soon as antenatal care is initiated. … For women with GDM, do not routinely measure HbA1c. … individualize glycaemic targets to optimize glycaemic control and improve maternal and neonatal outcomes.
conflicts: ADA 2026 sets fixed goals (fasting < 95 mg/dL, 1-h < 140, 2-h < 120; A1C < 6% if safe). WHO deliberately does not: 'The low certainty evidence identified through the review challenges the assumption that stricter glycaemic control always leads to better outcomes.'

claim: WHO 2025: for type 2 diabetes in pregnancy and for GDM not controlled by diet and physical activity, start metformin or insulin; medicines with safety concerns in pregnancy are replaced by insulin and/or metformin; type 1 continues its insulin.
document: WHO recommendations on care for women with diabetes during pregnancy
quote: For women with GDM who are unable to achieve optimal blood glucose levels with diet and physical activity alone, recommend initiation of metformin or insulin to optimize blood glucose control and outcomes for the woman and baby.
conflicts: CONFLICT: ADA states insulin is the preferred agent and that metformin and glyburide should not be first-line because they cross the placenta; WHO 2025 places metformin and insulin on an equal footing.

claim: WHO 2025: in type 1/type 2 diabetes, screen for retinopathy and assess renal function when antenatal care starts; keep BP below 130/80 mmHg if renal function is impaired; routine ultrasound before 24 weeks for all; none of the eye/renal checks routinely in GDM.
document: WHO recommendations on care for women with diabetes during pregnancy
quote: For pregnant women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes with impaired renal function, emphasize the importance of maintaining blood pressure levels below 130/80 mmHg during pregnancy and offer antihypertensives known to be safe in pregnancy as indicated.
conflicts: ADA: dilated eye exam before pregnancy/first trimester then every trimester and for 1 year postpartum as indicated; ADA BP goal in pregnancy with chronic hypertension is 110-135/85 mmHg (from memory, not opened). WHO: 'there is no standard timeframe for repeat screening'.

claim: After GDM, glucose-lowering treatment is usually stopped after birth and glucose tolerance must be re-assessed 6 to 12 weeks postnatally.
document: WHO recommendations on care for women with diabetes during pregnancy
section: Recommendations and supporting evidence - remarks to recommendations 17-18
quote: Due to the increased risk of type 2 diabetes in women who have experienced GDM, follow-up assessment of glucose tolerance is essential 6 to 12 weeks postnatally.
conflicts: CONFLICT: ADA says 75 g OGTT at 4-12 weeks postpartum then lifelong screening every 1-3 years; WHO/FIGO say 6-12 weeks. Engine window 6-12 weeks satisfies both.

claim: WHO 2025: pregnant women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes should receive multidisciplinary specialised care; for GDM this is 'consider', depending on access.
document: WHO recommendations on care for women with diabetes during pregnancy
quote: For pregnant women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, deliver multidisciplinary and specialized care provided by health-care providers trained in maternal and diabetes care.

claim: WHO 2016 ANC recommendation B.1.4 restates the 2013 classification and explicitly is not a recommendation on routine screening; the usual window for GDM diagnosis is 24-28 weeks.
document: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
conflicts: FIGO and ADA recommend universal testing at 24-28 weeks; WHO has no universal-screening recommendation.

claim: ADA: glucose goals in pregnancy (GDM and pre-existing diabetes) are fasting < 95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L) and either 1-h postprandial < 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) or 2-h postprandial < 120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L).
version: 2026 (wording not opened; values corroborated by StatPearls 2025)
document: 15. Management of Diabetes in Pregnancy: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026. Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S321
quote: The ADA and ACOG suggest a glucose target of less than 95 mg/dL fasting and 140 mg/dL postprandial or less at 1 hour or 120 mg/dL at 2 hours.
conflicts: WHO 2025 sets no numeric targets (individualise). WHO's evidence review quotes a 'two-hour postprandial target of <6.7 mmol/L (120 mg/dL)' among trial targets.

claim: ADA: preconception A1C ideally < 6.5% (48 mmol/mol); in pregnancy the ideal A1C goal is < 6% (42 mmol/mol) if achievable without significant hypoglycaemia, relaxed to < 7% (53 mmol/mol) if necessary to prevent hypoglycaemia.
document: 15. Management of Diabetes in Pregnancy: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026. Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S321
section: Section 15, preconception counselling and glycaemic goals
quote: Most organizations recommend women achieve an A1c of less than 6.5% prior to conception … (<6% if possible with minimal hypoglycemia)
conflicts: WHO 2025: measure HbA1c early in T1D/T2D but no numeric goal; HbA1c is physiologically lower in pregnancy and unreliable with anaemia/haemoglobinopathy (see A10 HbA1c items).

claim: ADA: potentially harmful medicines (ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, statins) should be stopped before conception and avoided in sexually active women of child-bearing potential not using reliable contraception.
document: 15. Management of Diabetes in Pregnancy: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026. Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S321
quote: Women who are taking ACE-inhibitors or ARBs should be counseled that these agents are contraindicated in the 2nd and 3rd trimester of pregnancy … Statins should be discontinued before conception
conflicts: WHO 2025 rec 27 says only 'antihypertensives known to be safe in pregnancy'; rec 15 says replace glucose-lowering medicines with safety concerns by insulin and/or metformin.

claim: ADA: insulin is the preferred agent for hyperglycaemia in pregnancy (type 1, type 2 and GDM); metformin and glyburide are not first-line because they cross the placenta.
document: 15. Management of Diabetes in Pregnancy: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026. Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S321
quote: Insulin does not cross the placental barrier and is recommended by the ADA for first-line treatment of GDM.
conflicts: CONFLICT with WHO 2025 recs 13 and 17 ('initiation of metformin or insulin'). For Uganda, WHO is the governing standard and metformin is on the national EML; the engine should present both and let the clinician choose.

claim: ADA: pregnant women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes should be prescribed low-dose aspirin starting at 12 to 16 weeks of gestation to lower the risk of pre-eclampsia.
document: 15. Management of Diabetes in Pregnancy: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026. Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S321
conflicts: USPSTF/ACOG: start between 12 and 28 weeks, optimally before 16 weeks. WHO ANC: low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks (before 20 weeks) for women at high risk of pre-eclampsia (from memory).

claim: ADA: women with pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes should have a dilated eye examination ideally before pregnancy and in the first trimester, then be monitored every trimester and for 1 year postpartum as indicated by the degree of retinopathy.
document: 15. Management of Diabetes in Pregnancy: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026. Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S321
conflicts: WHO 2025 rec 23: screen for retinopathy when antenatal care is initiated, follow-up by risk, 'no standard timeframe for repeat screening'; rec 24: do not routinely screen in GDM.

claim: ADA: after GDM, test with a 75 g OGTT at 4-12 weeks postpartum using non-pregnancy criteria, then screen lifelong for type 2 diabetes/prediabetes every 1-3 years.
document: 15. Management of Diabetes in Pregnancy: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026. Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S321
quote: guidelines recommend postpartum screening for all women who have GDM, ideally between 4 to 12 weeks after delivery. … Screen for diabetes every 1 to 3 years
conflicts: WHO 2025 and FIGO: 6-12 weeks postnatally (see A10-10).

claim: FIGO: all pregnant women should be tested for hyperglycaemia with a one-step procedure; FIGO adopts WHO 2013 criteria for diabetes in pregnancy and WHO 2013/IADPSG 2010 criteria for GDM.
document: The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) Initiative on gestational diabetes mellitus: A pragmatic guide for diagnosis, management, and care. Hod M et al. Int J Gynecol Obstet 2015;131(Suppl 3):S173-S211
quote: FIGO adopts and supports the IADPSG/WHO/IDF position that all pregnant women should be tested for hyperglycemia during pregnancy using a one-step procedure.
conflicts: WHO makes no universal-screening recommendation; ADA allows one-step or two-step.

claim: FIGO accepts pragmatic country-specific alternatives when the full fasting 75 g OGTT is not feasible, and recommends a plasma-calibrated handheld glucometer in primary care; e.g. India (DIPSI) uses a single 75 g 2-h value taken fasting or non-fasting, 7.8-11.0 mmol/L = GDM.
document: The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) Initiative on gestational diabetes mellitus: A pragmatic guide for diagnosis, management, and care. Hod M et al. Int J Gynecol Obstet 2015;131(Suppl 3):S173-S211
quote: Given the resource constraints in many low-resource countries, other strategies described herein are considered equally acceptable. … FIGO recommends the use of a plasma-calibrated handheld glucometer with properly stored test strips to measure plasma glucose in primary care settings
conflicts: These alternatives use different thresholds from WHO 2013 (e.g. 2-h 7.8 vs 8.5 mmol/L), so prevalence and labelling differ by strategy.

claim: FIGO Table 4: in fully resourced settings test all women at booking/first trimester and at 24-28 weeks; in basic/low-resource settings test all women between 24 and 28 weeks with a 75 g OGTT.
document: The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) Initiative on gestational diabetes mellitus: A pragmatic guide for diagnosis, management, and care. Hod M et al. Int J Gynecol Obstet 2015;131(Suppl 3):S173-S211
quote: diagnosis of GDM is made using a single-step 75-g OGTT when one or more of the following results are recorded during routine testing specifically between weeks 24 and 28 of pregnancy
conflicts: ADA: test women with risk factors before 15 weeks for undiagnosed diabetes, and all others at 24-28 weeks (Section 2, from memory).

claim: In a Kampala clinic, new-onset hyperglycaemia occurred in 16 of 3417 people switched to dolutegravir versus 1 of 3230 on non-DTG ART, a median of 4 months after starting; most cases were severe.
version: Lamorde M et al. Lancet HIV 2020;7(7):e461-e462
document: Dolutegravir-associated hyperglycaemia in patients with HIV
quote: 16/3417 (0·47%) … 1/3230 (0·03%) … Median time from starting dolutegravir to onset of hyperglycaemia was 4 months
conflicts: Later prospective Ugandan cohorts (A10-25, A10-26) found low diabetes incidence in ART-naive people starting DTG.

claim: Uganda MoH (2020 consolidated HIV guidelines, as cited by Mulindwa et al.): avoid DTG in people known to have diabetes, withhold it if type 2 diabetes develops, and check blood glucose every three months in those with age >= 45 years, raised BMI or hypertension.
document: Consolidated Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of HIV and AIDS in Uganda
section: 2020 edition as cited in Mulindwa F et al. AIDS Res Ther 2023;20:15 (ref 18); 2022 edition Figures 44 and 57
quote: the Uganda Ministry of Health (MoH) recommended avoiding the use of DTG in Ugandan ART naïve and experienced PLHIV known to have diabetes mellitus and withholding DTG in patients who develop type-2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Additionally, the guidelines encouraged three monthly blood glucose (BG) monitoring for patients with one or more of these factors; age ≥ 45 years, BMI ≥ 24 kg/m2
conflicts: A second paper by the same group (BMC Infect Dis 2024;24:746) describes the guidance as 'blood glucose monitoring every 3 months during the first six months of therapy in PWH with pre-diabetes mellitus'. WHO: no DTG-specific glucose-monitoring recommendation was located in this search.

claim: Prospective Ugandan cohort (GLUMED): among 243 ART-naive adults without diabetes started on DTG, 1 developed type 2 diabetes and 54 developed pre-diabetes over 48 weeks.
version: Mulindwa F et al. AIDS Res Ther 2023;20:15
document: Blood glucose trajectories and incidence of diabetes mellitus in Ugandan people living with HIV initiated on dolutegravir
quote: The incidence of T2DM was 4 cases per 1000 PY (1/243) and pre-DM, 240 cases per 1000 person years (PY) (54/243).
conflicts: Contrasts with Lamorde 2020 signal in ART-experienced switchers; authors conclude 'Restricting the use of dolutegravir in Ugandan ART naïve patients perceived to be high risk for diabetes mellitus may be unwarranted.'

claim: Ugandan ART-naive adults with pre-diabetes started on DTG did not worsen over 48 weeks; authors judge intensified early glucose monitoring unnecessary but long-term surveillance imperative.
version: Mulindwa F et al. BMC Infect Dis 2024;24:746
document: Blood glucose outcomes of anti-retroviral therapy naïve Ugandan people with HIV with pre-diabetes mellitus initiated on dolutegravir for 48 weeks
quote: Intensified blood glucose monitoring of these patients in the first six months of DTG anchored ART may be unnecessary but long-term diabetes surveillance is still imperative.
conflicts: MoH guidance (as cited) asked for 3-monthly glucose in the first six months for pre-diabetes.

claim: HbA1c underestimates glycaemia in people with HIV on ART; discordance is associated with low CD4 count, protease inhibitor or NNRTI regimens, zidovudine and raised MCV.
version: Slama L et al. J Antimicrob Chemother 2014;69(12):3360-3367
document: Inaccuracy of haemoglobin A1c among HIV-infected men: effects of CD4 cell count, antiretroviral therapies and haematological parameters
quote: HbA1c underestimates glycaemia in HIV-infected patients and its use in patients with risk factors for HbA1c discordance may lead to under-diagnosis and to under-treatment of established diabetes mellitus.
conflicts: ADA Section 2 advises using plasma glucose criteria rather than A1C to diagnose diabetes in people with HIV (from memory; not opened). Kim PS et al. Diabetes Care 2009;32:1591-3 ('Hemoglobin A1c underestimates glycemia in HIV infection') not opened.

claim: WHO's 2011 HbA1c consultation lists antiretrovirals among drugs that decrease HbA1c by shortening erythrocyte life span.
document: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus: Abbreviated Report of a WHO Consultation
section: Annex: Some of the factors that influence HbA1c and its measurement
quote: Decreased A1c: decreased erythrocyte life span: haemoglobinopathies, splenomegaly, rheumatoid arthritis or drugs such as antiretrovirals, ribavirin and dapsone.

claim: US DHHS adult ARV guidelines Table 20: diabetes/insulin resistance is listed for zidovudine among NRTIs and as 'rarely observed' for protease inhibitors; weight gain is greater with INSTIs, especially bictegravir and dolutegravir.
version: US DHHS Guidelines for the Use of Antiretroviral Agents in Adults and Adolescents With HIV (page updated 25 Sep 2025)
document: Adverse Effects of Antiretroviral Agents - Table 20. Common and/or Severe Adverse Effects Associated With Antiretroviral Medications
section: Row 'Diabetes Mellitus and Insulin Resistance'; row 'Weight Gain'
quote: Weight gain has been associated with initiation of ART and subsequent viral suppression. The increase appears to be greater with INSTIs, especially BIC and DTG, than with other drug classes.
conflicts: The DHHS 'no known effect' cell for INSTIs conflicts with the Ugandan DTG hyperglycaemia reports (A10-23) and with Uganda MoH caution. Older boosted PIs (lopinavir/ritonavir, indinavir) are the PIs historically linked to insulin resistance (from memory).

claim: WHO/The Union 2011 framework: TB patients should be screened for diabetes at the start of TB treatment where resources allow; people with diabetes should be asked about cough > 2 weeks at diagnosis and at check-ups.
document: Collaborative framework for care and control of tuberculosis and diabetes
quote: TB patients should be screened for diabetes at the start of TB treatment, where resources for diagnosis are available. … At a minimum, people with diabetes should be asked about the presence of cough (lasting more than 2 weeks) at the time of diabetes diagnosis, and if possible at each regular check-up for diabetes.

claim: WHO 2025 handbook: diabetes testing should be available to everyone in TB care who does not know their diabetes status; where universal testing is not possible prioritise adults with symptoms, those > 40 years who are overweight, and those who are obese.
document: WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis. Module 6: tuberculosis and comorbidities, third edition (diabetes chapter; ISBN 9789240103276; announced 7 Feb 2025)
section: Diabetes chapter 4.1 Diabetes screening and diagnosis
quote: Adults with TB who have symptoms of diabetes or are > 40 years and are overweight and those who are obese (according to BMI) should be prioritized for diabetes testing.
conflicts: 2011 framework said simply 'screen TB patients at start of treatment where resources are available'.

claim: TB can cause stress/infection-related hyperglycaemia at diagnosis; glycaemic status must be reassessed (the handbook says after 1 month) and an asymptomatic positive screen confirmed by a repeat test.
document: WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis. Module 6: tuberculosis and comorbidities, third edition (diabetes chapter; ISBN 9789240103276; announced 7 Feb 2025)
quote: Glucose levels can be elevated at the time of TB diagnosis due to stress or TB infection-related hyperglycaemia. … It is therefore critical to reassess the glycaemic status after 1 month as part of standard diabetes management.
conflicts: 2011 framework: 'TB may temporarily elevate blood glucose levels and result in false-positive diagnoses of diabetes if investigations are performed too early.' Many programmes repeat at 2-3 months or at end of TB treatment (The Union guide) - the brief expected 'repeat after treatment'.

claim: WHO recommends systematic TB screening of people with a risk factor such as diabetes who are seeking or in care where general-population TB prevalence is 100/100 000 or higher; prioritise newly diagnosed diabetes and uncontrolled glycaemia.
document: WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis. Module 6: tuberculosis and comorbidities, third edition (diabetes chapter; ISBN 9789240103276; announced 7 Feb 2025)
section: Diabetes chapter 3.1 TB screening among people living with diabetes
quote: WHO recommends systematic screening for TB of people with a risk factor, who are either seeking health care or who are already in care in settings where TB prevalence among the general population is 100/100 000 or higher and diabetes is listed as one of the risk factors.
conflicts: WHO 2021 screening guideline wording is a conditional 'may be conducted' recommendation.

claim: Rifampicin induces hepatic metabolism of sulfonylureas and lowers their plasma levels; it may increase metformin's glucose-lowering effect; insulin is not affected.
document: WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis. Module 6: tuberculosis and comorbidities, third edition (diabetes chapter; ISBN 9789240103276; announced 7 Feb 2025)
section: Diabetes chapter 3.3 TB treatment among people living with diabetes; 4.2 Management of diabetes
quote: Rifampicin is a potent hepatic enzyme inducer, increasing the hepatic metabolism of sulfonylurea derivatives and therefore lowering their plasma levels. … The glucose-lowering effect of metformin may be increased by rifampicin.

claim: People with diabetes are at higher risk of peripheral neuropathy and optic neuritis from isoniazid, linezolid, cycloserine and ethambutol; pyridoxine prophylaxis prevents most neuropathy except that from linezolid.
document: WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis. Module 6: tuberculosis and comorbidities, third edition (diabetes chapter; ISBN 9789240103276; announced 7 Feb 2025)
quote: People living with diabetes are at increased risk of optic neuritis and peripheral neuropathy, which may be further exacerbated by exposure to linezolid, isoniazid or cycloserine. … Pyridoxine prophylaxis can help to prevent most cases of neuropathy, with the exception of linezolid.

claim: During TB treatment WHO keeps metformin as the initial glucose-lowering medicine and allows a more lenient HbA1c target (e.g. < 8%) than the usual about 7%.
document: WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis. Module 6: tuberculosis and comorbidities, third edition (diabetes chapter; ISBN 9789240103276; announced 7 Feb 2025)
quote: While glycaemic control to achieve an HbA1c of about 7% is generally recommended, … more lenient HbA1c target (e.g. < 8%) … Metformin is the recommended initial glucose-lowering medication

claim: People without known diabetes started on glucocorticoids: check capillary glucose at least once daily, preferably before lunch or evening meal (or 1-2 h after); if any reading exceeds 12.0 mmol/L test four times daily.
document: Management of Hyperglycaemia and Steroid (Glucocorticoid) Therapy. Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care (JBDS-IP) guideline 08, revised May 2021
quote: Monitor blood glucose at least once daily – preferably prior to lunch or evening meal, or alternatively 1-2 hours post lunch or evening meal … If a subsequent capillary blood glucose is found to be greater than 12.0mmol/L, then increase the frequency of testing to four times daily
conflicts: ADA Section 16 (not opened) advises glucose monitoring for inpatients on glucocorticoids and notes afternoon/evening hyperglycaemia with morning intermediate-acting steroids.

claim: People with diabetes started on glucocorticoids should test four times a day (before or after meals and before bed), irrespective of prior control.
document: Management of Hyperglycaemia and Steroid (Glucocorticoid) Therapy. Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care (JBDS-IP) guideline 08, revised May 2021
quote: Test four times a day, before or after meals, and before bed, irrespective of background diabetes control

claim: With morning prednisolone, glucose rises by late morning and stays high into the evening, falling back overnight; JBDS calls a steroid-related rise in someone without known diabetes 'steroid induced diabetes'; HbA1c screening should wait until 3 months after stopping steroids.
document: Management of Hyperglycaemia and Steroid (Glucocorticoid) Therapy. Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care (JBDS-IP) guideline 08, revised May 2021
quote: Given the recent hyperglycaemia the use of HbA1c as a screening tool should be delayed until 3 months following steroid cessation.

claim: JBDS inpatient glucose target on steroids: 6.0-10.0 mmol/L, accepting 6.0-12.0 mmol/L (2021 revision); the 2014 edition accepted 4-12 mmol/L.
document: Management of Hyperglycaemia and Steroid (Glucocorticoid) Therapy. Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care (JBDS-IP) guideline 08, revised May 2021
quote: The recommended target level for glucose in hospital inpatients is 6.0-10.0mmol/L, accepting a range of 6.0-12.0mmol/L.
conflicts: Edition conflict: lower acceptable bound moved from 4 to 6 mmol/L. ADA inpatient target is 140-180 mg/dL (7.8-10.0 mmol/L) (from memory).

claim: ADA/APA/AACE/NAASO 2004 consensus: screen before starting a second-generation antipsychotic; weight at 4, 8 and 12 weeks then quarterly; fasting glucose, lipids and BP at 12 weeks (3 months), then glucose and BP annually; clozapine and olanzapine carry the highest diabetes risk.
document: Consensus Development Conference on Antipsychotic Drugs and Obesity and Diabetes
section: Table: monitoring protocol for patients on SGAs
quote: fasting glucose levels, lipid levels and blood pressure be assessed three months after the initiation … blood pressure and plasma glucose values can be obtained annually or more frequently for patients at higher risk … Clozapine and olanzapine (Zyprexa) are associated with the greatest weight gain and highest occurrence of diabetes and dyslipidemia
conflicts: ADA Standards (Section 2/5; not opened) now word this as screening at baseline, 12-16 weeks after initiation and annually thereafter (from memory).

claim: Proposed criteria for type 3c (pancreatogenic) diabetes: all of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, pathological pancreatic imaging and absent type 1 autoimmune markers, supported by minor criteria; about 5-10% of diabetes in Western populations and usually misclassified as type 2.
version: Ewald N, Hardt PD. World J Gastroenterol 2013;19(42):7276-7281
document: Diagnosis and treatment of diabetes mellitus in chronic pancreatitis
section: Proposed diagnostic criteria for type 3c diabetes
quote: Presence of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (monoclonal fecal elastase-1 test or direct function tests) … Pathological pancreatic imaging (endoscopic ultrasound, MRI, CT) … Absence of type 1 diabetes mellitus associated autoimmune markers
conflicts: WHO 2019 classification lists 'diseases of the exocrine pancreas' (incl. fibrocalculous pancreatopathy, pancreatitis, trauma/pancreatectomy, neoplasia, cystic fibrosis, haemochromatosis) among 'other specific types' - WHO PDF could not be opened (IRIS 403).

claim: FCPD is diabetes due to non-alcoholic chronic calcific pancreatitis in the tropics: a lean adolescent/young adult with recurrent abdominal pain and steatorrhoea, large pancreatic calculi on plain X-ray or ultrasound, insulin-requiring but ketosis-resistant diabetes, and a raised risk of pancreatic cancer.
version: Unnikrishnan R, Mohan V. Acta Diabetol 2015;52:1-9
document: Fibrocalculous pancreatic diabetes (FCPD)
quote: The typical patient with FCPD is a lean adolescent or young adult of either sex, presenting with history of recurrent bouts of abdominal pain and steatorrhea. Demonstration of large, discrete pancreatic calculi by plain radiographs or ultrasonography of the abdomen is diagnostic.
conflicts: Type 5 (malnutrition-related) diabetes is distinguished by a NORMAL pancreas on imaging (A10-44).

claim: Type 5 (malnutrition-related) diabetes: lean (BMI < 18.5 kg/m2), young-onset (< 30 years) diabetes with early-life undernutrition, low C-peptide, ketosis resistance, no clinical insulin resistance, GAD-65 antibody negative and a normal pancreas on imaging.
standard: other (international consensus statement, Lancet Glob Health 2025)
version: 2025 consensus statement (Vellore, Jan 2025; IDF World Diabetes Congress, Apr 2025)
document: Wadivkar P, Jebasingh F, Thomas N, et al. Classifying a distinct form of diabetes in lean individuals with a history of undernutrition: an international consensus statement. Lancet Glob Health 2025;13(10):e1771-e1776
section: Summary; panel of commonly/occasionally reported features
quote: Since 1955, a form of diabetes in lean, young (BMI <18·5 kg/m2, age <30 years) individuals with a history suggestive of undernutrition from before birth and throughout childhood has been described in the literature.
conflicts: The brief suggested 'BMI < 18.5-19'; the consensus states < 18.5 kg/m2. WHO removed 'malnutrition-related diabetes mellitus' from its classification in 1999 and the 2019 WHO classification does not include type 5 (from memory). IDF news uses 20 to 25 million; the consensus says 25 million.

claim: There are no formal diagnostic criteria for type 5 diabetes yet: IDF launched a working group (15 April 2025) to develop them, and the consensus statement says its cut-offs need further research.
document: IDF launches new type 5 diabetes working group (IDF news, 15 April 2025)
section: News item; and Lancet Glob Health consensus statement
quote: develop formal diagnostic criteria and therapeutic guidelines for a type of diabetes linked to malnutrition
conflicts: Not recognised in WHO 2019 or ADA classifications.

claim: Ketosis-prone (Flatbush) diabetes: diabetes presenting with ketoacidosis in islet-antibody-negative, usually middle-aged, overweight, often male people of African ancestry; after initial intensive insulin many become insulin independent within weeks to months and follow a type 2 course.
version: Lebovitz HE, Banerji MA. Curr Diab Rep 2018;18:120
document: Ketosis-Prone Diabetes (Flatbush Diabetes): an Emerging Worldwide Clinically Important Entity
quote: KPD is defined as a syndrome in which diabetes commences with ketoacidosis in individuals who are GAD and anti-islet cell antibody negative … After intensive initial insulin therapy, many patients become insulin independent and can be well controlled on diet alone or diet plus oral medications
conflicts: WHO 2019 classification lists 'ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes' under 'hybrid forms of diabetes' - WHO PDF not opened (IRIS 403), so WHO's own wording is not recorded.

claim: In 568 Ugandan adults with newly diagnosed diabetes, 6.4% were islet-autoantibody positive; of the antibody-negative remainder 32% were lean (BMI < 25 kg/m2), and their diabetes was driven by reduced insulin secretion rather than insulin resistance, more often in men.
document: Understanding the pathogenesis of lean non-autoimmune diabetes in an African population with newly diagnosed diabetes
quote: 160 (32%) and 340 (68%) were lean and non-lean, respectively … Diabetes in these lean individuals was more common in men, and predominantly associated with reduced pancreatic secretory function rather than insulin resistance.
conflicts: ADA/EASD type 1 algorithm uses BMI < 25 as a pointer to type 1 - in Uganda a third of non-autoimmune adult-onset diabetes is lean, so BMI is a weak discriminator (the Holt algorithm is explicitly 'based on data from White European populations').

claim: In 894 young people with clinically diagnosed type 1 diabetes in Cameroon, Uganda and South Africa, only 34.9% were islet-autoantibody positive; the remaining 65.1% had a non-autoimmune, insulin-deficient form.
version: Katte JC et al. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2025;13(9):745-753
document: Non-autoimmune, insulin-deficient diabetes in children and young adults in Africa: evidence from the Young-Onset Diabetes in sub-Saharan Africa (YODA) cross-sectional study
quote: Only 312 (34·9%) of 894 participants were positive for islet autoantibodies … In sub-Saharan Africa, clinically diagnosed type 1 diabetes is heterogeneous, comprising classic autoimmune type 1 diabetes and a novel, non-autoimmune, insulin-deficient diabetes subtype.
conflicts: ADA/EASD: 5-10% of White European new-onset type 1 are antibody-negative - versus about 65% here.

claim: ADA/EASD: features pointing to type 1 diabetes in a newly diagnosed adult are age < 35 years (most discriminative), BMI < 25 kg/m2, unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis and glucose > 20 mmol/L (360 mg/dL); no single feature confirms type 1.
document: Holt RIG, DeVries JH, Hess-Fischl A, et al. The management of type 1 diabetes in adults. A consensus report by the American Diabetes Association (ADA) and the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD). Diabetologia 2021;64:2609-2652 (co-published Diabetes Care 2021;44:2589-2625)
section: Diagnosis of type 1 diabetes; Fig. 1 and footnotes
quote: younger age at diagnosis (<35 years), with lower BMI (<25 kg/m2), unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis and glucose >20 mmol/l (>360 mg/dl)
conflicts: Figure caption: 'based on data from White European populations' - Ugandan data (A10-47, A10-48) show lean and ketosis-prone non-autoimmune forms are common, so these discriminators perform worse locally.

claim: ADA/EASD: measure GAD antibodies first; if negative follow with IA-2 and/or ZnT8; 5-10% of White European new-onset type 1 are antibody negative, so a negative result does not exclude type 1 in those < 35 years.
document: Holt RIG, DeVries JH, Hess-Fischl A, et al. The management of type 1 diabetes in adults. A consensus report by the American Diabetes Association (ADA) and the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD). Diabetologia 2021;64:2609-2652 (co-published Diabetes Care 2021;44:2589-2625)
quote: GAD should be the primary antibody measured and, if negative, should be followed by islet tyrosine phosphatase 2 (IA2) and/or zinc transporter 8 (ZNT8)
conflicts: YODA (A10-48): about 65% of clinically diagnosed young type 1 in sub-Saharan Africa are antibody negative.

claim: ADA/EASD: C-peptide is used only in insulin-treated people, ideally beyond 3 years from diagnosis when type is uncertain; > 600 pmol/L strongly suggests type 2, 200-600 pmol/L is indeterminate (type 1, MODY or insulin-treated type 2), < 200 pmol/L indicates type 1; < 80 pmol/L needs no repeat.
document: Holt RIG, DeVries JH, Hess-Fischl A, et al. The management of type 1 diabetes in adults. A consensus report by the American Diabetes Association (ADA) and the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD). Diabetologia 2021;64:2609-2652 (co-published Diabetes Care 2021;44:2589-2625)

topic: FPG alone vs FPG + 2-h OGTT in sub-Saharan Africa
claim: In community screening of 1550 adults in Ethiopia and Nigeria, fasting plasma glucose alone missed 44.4% (32 of 72) of diabetes cases and 34.1% of prediabetes found when a 2-h OGTT was added.

claim: In 1190 urban Black South Africans, HbA1c >= 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) detected OGTT-defined diabetes with 70.3% sensitivity and 98.7% specificity; the ROC-optimal cut-off was 6.0% (42 mmol/mol).

topic: HbA1c >= 6.5% pooled accuracy in Africa (Chivese meta-analysis)

quote: Eleven studies from seven African countries with 12,925 participants were included. Against OGTT, HbA1c had pooled sensitivity 57.7% (95% CI 43.4–70.9) and specificity 92.3% (95% CI 83.9–96.5). ... In Africa, HbA1c may miss almost half of individuals with T2D based on blood glucose measures.
conflicts: WHO 2011 / ADA 2026 keep 6.5% as the diagnostic threshold. Royce 2024 paraphrases this paper as 'missed up to 42% and 35%' of OGTT- and FPG-defined diabetes (i.e. 100 - 57.7 and 100 - 64.5).

version: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026; Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S27-S49
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: When using OGTT as a screening tool for prediabetes or diabetes, adequate carbohydrate intake (at least 150 g/day) should be assured for 3 days prior to testing. ... People should follow a mixed eating pattern with at least 150 g of carbohydrates on the 3 days prior to OGTT

claim: Fasting plasma glucose varies within the same person by about 5-6% between occasions (within-person variability 5.7% for FPG measured 2 to 4 weeks apart), which is why a value near the threshold needs repeating.
document: Guidelines and Recommendations for Laboratory Analysis in the Diagnosis and Management of Diabetes Mellitus (Sacks DB, Arnold M, Bakris GL, Bruns DE, Horvath AR, Lernmark A, Metzger BE, Nathan DM, Kirkman MS)
quote: within- and between-subject CVs of 4.8% to 6.1% and 7.5% to 7.8%, respectively ... mean within-person variability of FPG measured 2 to 4 weeks apart was 5.7% ... analytical imprecision ≤2.4%, bias ≤2.1% and total error ≤6.1%

claim: Fasting capillary and venous glucose differ by only about 0.1 mmol/L (2 mg/dL), but after a glucose load capillary values are significantly higher (mean about 1.7 mmol/L or 30 mg/dL).
document: Guidelines and Recommendations for Laboratory Analysis in the Diagnosis and Management of Diabetes Mellitus (Sacks DB, Arnold M, Bakris GL, Bruns DE, Horvath AR, Lernmark A, Metzger BE, Nathan DM, Kirkman MS)
quote: glucose concentrations in capillary (fingerstick) blood are significantly higher than those in venous blood (mean of 1.7 mmol/L or 30 mg/dL) ... mean difference in fasting samples is only 0.1 mmol/L (2 mg/dL)

topic: HbA1c and FPG accuracy vs OGTT in Uganda
claim: In outpatients aged 30-75 at a general hospital in eastern Uganda, HbA1c at 6.5% had 69.8% sensitivity and FPG at 7.0 mmol/L had 62.6% sensitivity for OGTT-defined diabetes; both were highly specific (98.6% and 99.4%).
document: Glycated haemoglobin and fasting plasma glucose tests in the screening of outpatients for diabetes and abnormal glucose regulation in Uganda: A diagnostic accuracy study (Kasujja FX, Mayega RW, Daivadanam M, Kiracho EE, Kusolo R, Nuwaha F)
quote: At recommended cut-off points for diabetes, the HBA1C and FPG tests had comparable sensitivity [69.8% (95% CI 46.3–86.1) versus 62.6% (95% CI 41.5–79.8), respectively] and specificity [98.6% (95% CI 95.4–99.6) versus 99.4% (95% CI 98.9–99.7), respectively].
conflicts: Study-proposed optimum cut-offs (HbA1c 6.3%; FPG 6.4 mmol/L) differ from WHO/ADA diagnostic thresholds (6.5%; 7.0 mmol/L) and are not diagnostic criteria.

claim: In 4027 Kenyan adults (STEPS 2015), modified and simplified FINDRISC detected undiagnosed diabetes (fasting capillary glucose >= 7.0 mmol/L) with AUC about 0.75; at the optimal cut-off >= 7 the simplified score's PPV was only 7.9%.
document: Performance of a Finnish Diabetes Risk Score in detecting undiagnosed diabetes among Kenyans aged 18-69 years (Mugume IB, Wafula ST, Kadengye DT, Van Olmen J)
quote: The AU-ROC of the modified FINDRISC and simplified FINDRISC in detecting undiagnosed diabetes were 0.7481 and 0.7486 respectively ... With an optimal cut-off ≥ 7, the simplified FINDRISC had a higher positive predictive value (PPV) (7.9%) and diagnostic odds (OR:6.65, 95%CI: 4.43–9.96)
conflicts: Optimal cut-off in Kenya (>= 7) is far below the Finnish action thresholds (>= 12 or >= 15), i.e. the Finnish bands do not transfer.

topic: HbA1c: shortened red-cell survival lowers results regardless of assay (NGSP)
claim: NGSP states that any condition that shortens erythrocyte survival or lowers mean erythrocyte age (e.g. recovery from acute blood loss, haemolytic anaemia) falsely lowers HbA1c regardless of assay method.
version: NGSP web page, last updated 23 June 2026 as displayed
document: NGSP: Factors that Interfere with HbA1c Test Results
quote: Any condition that shortens erythrocyte survival or decreases mean erythrocyte age (e.g., recovery from acute blood loss ...) will falsely lower HbA1c test results regardless of the assay method ... HbA1c results from patients with HbSS, HbCC, and HbSC must be interpreted with caution

topic: HbA1c: haemoglobin variants and HbF interfere by assay method (NGSP)
claim: NGSP states that genetic variants (e.g. HbS trait, HbC trait), elevated HbF and chemically modified haemoglobin (e.g. carbamylated Hb in renal failure) can affect HbA1c accuracy, with the direction depending on the specific assay method.
version: NGSP web page, last updated 23 June 2026 as displayed
document: NGSP: Factors that Interfere with HbA1c Test Results
quote: Genetic variants (e.g. HbS trait, HbC trait) ... elevated fetal hemoglobin (HbF) and chemically modified derivatives of hemoglobin (e.g. carbamylated Hb in patients with renal failure) can affect the accuracy of HbA1c measurements.

topic: HbA1c: iron deficiency raises, iron therapy lowers (NGSP)
claim: NGSP states iron-deficiency anaemia is associated with higher HbA1c (and higher fructosamine), iron replacement lowers both, and HbA1c rises in late pregnancy in non-diabetic women owing to iron deficiency.
version: NGSP web page, last updated 23 June 2026 as displayed
document: NGSP: Factors that Interfere with HbA1c Test Results
quote: Iron deficiency anemia ... is associated with higher HbA1c and higher fructosamine ... Iron replacement therapy lowers both HbA1c and fructosamine concentrations in diabetic and non-diabetic individuals ... HbA1c ... is increased in late pregnancy in nondiabetic individuals owing to iron deficiency
conflicts: The brief lists pregnancy 2nd/3rd trimester as 'falsely low' (the ADA position: increased red cell turnover lowers A1C in pregnancy). NGSP says late-pregnancy HbA1c rises through iron deficiency. Both effects exist; net direction in a given pregnant Ugandan woman is unpredictable, so glucose criteria should be used in pregnancy (ADA Rec 2.4).

claim: NGSP notes reports that HbA1c underestimates glycaemia in people with diabetes on dialysis and that glycated albumin is a more robust indicator; the roles of renal anaemia and erythropoietin are harder to evaluate.
version: NGSP web page, last updated 23 June 2026 as displayed
document: NGSP: Factors that Interfere with HbA1c Test Results
quote: Recent reports suggest HbA1c underestimates glycemic control in diabetic patients on dialysis and that glycated albumin is ... robust ... the role of renal anemia, erythropoietin intake, and other factors in chronic renal failure is more difficult to evaluate

topic: WHO list of factors influencing HbA1c - erythropoiesis and red-cell survival
claim: WHO 2011 Annex 1: HbA1c is increased by iron or vitamin B12 deficiency, decreased erythropoiesis and splenectomy; decreased by erythropoietin, iron or B12 administration, reticulocytosis, chronic liver disease, and by shortened red-cell life span (haemoglobinopathies, splenomegaly, rheumatoid arthritis, antiretrovirals, ribavirin, dapsone).
document: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus: Abbreviated Report of a WHO Consultation
section: Annex 1: Some of the factors that influence HbA1c and its measurement (adapted from Gallagher et al.)
quote: Increased HbA1c: iron, vitamin B12 deficiency, decreased erythropoiesis. Decreased HbA1c: administration of erythropoietin, iron, vitamin B12, reticulocytosis, chronic liver disease. ... increased erythrocyte life span: Splenectomy. Decreased HbA1c: decreased erythrocyte life span: haemoglobinopathies, splenomegaly, rheumatoid arthritis or drugs such as antiretrovirals, ribavirin and dapsone.

topic: WHO list of factors influencing HbA1c - glycation and assay interference
claim: WHO 2011 Annex 1: glycation is increased by alcoholism and chronic renal failure and decreased by aspirin and vitamins C and E; assay results are increased by hyperbilirubinaemia, carbamylated haemoglobin, alcoholism, large doses of aspirin and chronic opiate use, and DECREASED by hypertriglyceridaemia.
document: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus: Abbreviated Report of a WHO Consultation
quote: Increased HbA1c: alcoholism, chronic renal failure, decreased intra-erythrocyte pH. Decreased HbA1c: aspirin, vitamin C and E, certain haemoglobinopathies, increased intra-erythrocyte pH. ... Increased HbA1c: hyperbilirubinaemia, carbamylated haemoglobin, alcoholism, large doses of aspirin, chronic opiate use. Variable HbA1c: haemoglobinopathies. Decreased HbA1c: hypertriglyceridaemia.
conflicts: The brief (and several textbooks) list severe hypertriglyceridaemia as causing FALSELY HIGH HbA1c; the WHO annex lists hypertriglyceridaemia under DECREASED HbA1c (assay effect). Direction is assay-dependent; the engine should flag 'unreliable', not assert a direction.

topic: ADA: when to use plasma glucose instead of A1C
claim: ADA 2026 says plasma glucose criteria should be used to diagnose diabetes in conditions with an altered A1C-glycaemia relationship (some haemoglobin variants, pregnancy, G6PD deficiency, HIV, altered red blood cell turnover) and that A1C may be unsuitable in anaemia, erythropoietin treatment, haemodialysis or HIV treatment.
version: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026; Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S27-S49
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: In conditions associated with an altered relationship between A1C and glycemia, such as some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, HIV, and conditions that may alter red blood cell turnover, plasma glucose criteria should be used to diagnose diabetes.

topic: ADA: G6PD variant and ancestry effects on A1C
claim: ADA 2026 cites that the X-linked G6PD G202A variant, carried by 11% of Black individuals in the US, lowers A1C by about 0.8%, and that Black individuals have slightly higher A1C (about 0.3%) than non-Hispanic White or Hispanic people at similar glycaemia.
version: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026; Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S27-S49
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Another genetic variant, X-linked glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase G202A, carried by 11% of Black individuals in the U.S., is associated with a decrease in A1C of about 0.8% ... Studies have found that Black individuals have slightly higher A1C levels (approximately 0.3%) than non-Hispanic White or Hispanic people

topic: ADLM/ADA: red-cell turnover, variants and homozygous variants
claim: The ADLM/ADA laboratory guideline states HbA1c in disorders affecting red-cell turnover gives spurious (generally falsely low) results regardless of method, that variant interference is method-dependent, and that HbA1c cannot be measured and should not be reported in people without HbA (homozygous variants).
document: Executive Summary: Guidelines and Recommendations for Laboratory Analysis in the Diagnosis and Management of Diabetes Mellitus (Sacks DB, et al.)
quote: Hb A1c measurements in individuals with disorders that affect red blood cell turnover may provide spurious (generally falsely low) results regardless of the method used. ... Hb A1c cannot be measured and should not be reported in individuals who do not have Hb A, e.g., those with homozygous hemoglobin variants.

topic: WHO: HbA1c < 6.5% does not exclude diabetes
claim: WHO 2011 recommends HbA1c 6.5% as the diagnostic cut point only with stringent quality assurance, standardised assays and no condition precluding accurate measurement, and states that a value below 6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed by glucose tests.
document: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus: Abbreviated Report of a WHO Consultation
quote: An HbA1c of 6.5% is recommended as the cut point for diagnosing diabetes. A value of less than 6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed using glucose tests.

claim: ADA 2026 recommends an A1C test on everyone admitted with diabetes or with hyperglycaemia (random blood glucose > 7.8 mmol/L) if no A1C result is available from the prior 3 months; hospital hyperglycaemia is any glucose > 7.8 mmol/L and an admission A1C >= 6.5% suggests diabetes preceded admission.
version: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026; Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S339-S355
document: 16. Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Perform an A1C test on all people with diabetes or hyperglycemia (random blood glucose >140 mg/dL [>7.8 mmol/L]) at the time of admission to the hospital if no A1C test result is available from the prior 3 months. ... An admission A1C value ≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol) suggests that the onset of diabetes preceded hospitalization.
conflicts: Endocrine Society 2012 uses a 2-3 month look-back; NICE NG185 defines post-ACS hyperglycaemia at > 11.0 mmol/L, not 7.8.

topic: Inpatient hyperglycaemia: Endocrine Society 2012 recognition steps
claim: The Endocrine Society (2012) suggests laboratory glucose on admission for all patients, bedside monitoring for 24-48 h in those without known diabetes whose glucose exceeds 7.8 mmol/L, and HbA1c in all inpatients with known diabetes or hyperglycaemia if not done in the preceding 2-3 months.
version: Endocrine Society 2012; J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2012;97(1):16-38
document: Management of Hyperglycemia in Hospitalized Patients in Non-Critical Care Setting: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (Umpierrez GE, et al.)
quote: We recommend that patients without a history of diabetes with BG greater than 7.8 mmol/liter (140 mg/dl) be monitored with bedside POC testing for at least 24 to 48 h. ... We recommend that all inpatients with known diabetes or with hyperglycemia (>7.8 mmol/liter) be assessed with a hemoglobin A1C level if this has not been performed in the preceding 2–3 months.
conflicts: ADA 2026 uses a 3-month look-back. The 2022 Endocrine Society update (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2022;107:2101-2128, opened) does not restate these recognition steps; it keeps BG > 140 mg/dL as the hyperglycaemia threshold.

topic: Stress hyperglycaemia: definition and HbA1c to separate it from undiagnosed diabetes
claim: The Endocrine Society describes stress hyperglycaemia as hyperglycaemia during acute illness that resolves by the time of discharge; in newly recognised hyperglycaemia an HbA1c of 6.5% or higher identifies diabetes, and an HbA1c helps separate undiagnosed diabetes from stress hyperglycaemia.
version: Endocrine Society 2012; J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2012;97(1):16-38
document: Management of Hyperglycemia in Hospitalized Patients in Non-Critical Care Setting: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (Umpierrez GE, et al.)
quote: ... those with previously undiagnosed diabetes and others with 'stress hyperglycemia' that may occur during an acute illness and that resolves by the time of discharge. ... In patients with newly recognized hyperglycemia, an HbA1C may help differentiate patients with previously undiagnosed diabetes from those with stress-induced hyperglycemia

topic: Hyperglycaemia after acute coronary syndrome: retest after recovery (NICE)
claim: NICE defines hyperglycaemia in ACS as blood glucose above 11.0 mmol/L and, for those without known diabetes, offers HbA1c before discharge and a fasting blood glucose no earlier than 4 days after ACS onset, with at least annual testing thereafter; OGTT is not routinely offered if both are normal.
document: Acute coronary syndromes (NICE guideline NG185)
section: Recs 1.3.1-1.3.5 (as numbered by the fetch tool; check section numbering)
quote: fasting blood glucose levels no earlier than 4 days after the onset of acute coronary syndrome ... Do not routinely offer oral glucose tolerance tests to people with hyperglycaemia after acute coronary syndrome and without known diabetes if HbA1c and fasting blood glucose levels are within the normal range.
conflicts: NICE threshold for 'hyperglycaemia' in ACS is > 11.0 mmol/L; ADA/Endocrine Society inpatient threshold is > 7.8 mmol/L.

topic: WHO HEARTS-D / WHO PEN: who to test and risk-score statement
claim: WHO HEARTS-D (2020) and WHO PEN (2020) could not be opened in this domain, so their who-to-test criteria, any statement on risk scores, the random-glucose algorithm threshold and the WHO re-screening interval are NOT verified here.
document: HEARTS D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
quote: HEARTS D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes

topic: Re-screening interval after a normal test (ADA)
claim: ADA 2026: if results are normal, repeat testing at a minimum of 3-year intervals; people with prediabetes are tested yearly and those with prior GDM at least every 1-3 years; results close to the threshold should be repeated in 3-6 months.
version: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026; Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S27-S49
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: If results are normal, testing should be repeated at a minimum of 3-year intervals ... People with prediabetes (A1C ≥5.7% [≥39 mmol/mol], IGT, or IFG) should be tested yearly. ... People who were diagnosed with GDM should have testing at least every 1–3 years. ... For all other people, testing should begin at age 35 years.
conflicts: WHO interval not verified in this domain (HEARTS-D not opened; about every 3 years from memory). NICE after ACS hyperglycaemia: at least annually.

topic: What is needed to exclude diabetes in a high-risk African patient
claim: No guideline was found that states which combination of tests excludes diabetes in a high-risk African adult; the evidence retrieved shows each single test misses a third or more of OGTT-defined cases, so a single normal FPG or HbA1c is only a weak negative and a 2-h OGTT is the most sensitive test.
version: Synthesis of items in this file (2011-2026 sources)
document: Synthesis: WHO 2011 HbA1c report; ADA 2026 Section 2; Kasujja 2022; Baye 2025; Chivese 2022
quote: A value of less than 6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed using glucose tests.

topic: IDF waist circumference cut-offs for sub-Saharan Africans
claim: The IDF 2006 metabolic syndrome consensus gives no African-specific waist cut-off: for sub-Saharan Africans it says to use European data (men >= 94 cm, women >= 80 cm) until more specific data are available.
document: The IDF consensus worldwide definition of the metabolic syndrome
quote: Sub-Saharan Africans: "Use European data until more specific data are available" ... Europids: "Male ≥ 94 cm / Female ≥ 80 cm" ... "If BMI is >30kg/m², central obesity can be assumed and waist circumference does not need to be measured"
conflicts: IDF metabolic-syndrome FPG component is 5.6 mmol/L (ADA IFG threshold), not the WHO IFG threshold of 6.1 mmol/L. Ekoru 2018 proposes about 81 cm for both sexes in SSA (next item).

topic: Proposed sub-Saharan African waist circumference threshold (Ekoru 2018)
claim: Pooled data on 24 181 adults from 17 studies in 8 SSA countries (including Uganda) gave an optimal waist cut-point for detecting cardiometabolic risk of 81.2 cm in men and 81.0 cm in women, i.e. far below the 94 cm European value for men.
document: Deriving an optimal threshold of waist circumference for detecting cardiometabolic risk in sub-Saharan Africa (Ekoru K, Murphy GAV, Young EH, et al.)
quote: The optimal WC cut-point was 81.2 cm (95% CI 78.5–83.8 cm) and 81.0 cm (95% CI 79.2–82.8 cm) for men and women, respectively ... The optimal WC cut-point for identifying men at increased cardiometabolic risk is lower (⩾81.2 cm) than current guidelines (⩾94.0 cm) recommend
conflicts: IDF 2006: 94 cm men / 80 cm women for sub-Saharan Africans (European values). For women the two agree (80 vs 81 cm); for men they differ by about 13 cm.

topic: ADA risk-factor list for testing asymptomatic adults
claim: ADA 2026 Table 2.5: consider testing adults with overweight/obesity plus one or more risk factors - first-degree relative with diabetes, high-risk ancestry, CVD history, hypertension, low HDL/high triglycerides, PCOS, physical inactivity, or other insulin-resistance conditions such as severe obesity, acanthosis nigricans and MASLD.
version: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026; Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S27-S49
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Testing should be considered in adults with overweight or obesity (BMI ≥25 kg/m2 or ≥23 kg/m2 in individuals of Asian ancestry) who have one or more of the following risk factors: ... Individuals with polycystic ovary syndrome ... Other clinical conditions associated with insulin resistance (e.g., severe obesity, acanthosis nigricans, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease)
conflicts: ADA gates risk-factor testing on overweight/obesity; in sub-Saharan Africa a large share of people with type 2 diabetes are not overweight (Baye 2025 recommends 2-h PG in 'non-obese persons who would be missed'), so a BMI gate would under-test Ugandans. ADA hypertension definition (>= 130/80) differs from the >= 140/90 used in Uganda STEPS and ADRS derivation.

claim: ADA 2026 advises considering screening in people on statins, thiazide diuretics and some HIV medications, screening at baseline and 12-16 weeks after starting second-generation antipsychotics, FPG screening in people with HIV before and 3-6 months after starting or switching ART, and monitoring glucose with long-term glucocorticoids.
version: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026; Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S27-S49
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Recs 2.16-2.18 (as numbered by the fetch tool)
quote: People with HIV should be screened for diabetes and prediabetes with an FPG test before starting antiretroviral therapy, at the time of switching antiretroviral therapy, and 3–6 months after starting or switching antiretroviral therapy.

topic: Periodontal disease and diabetes: two-way link
claim: ADA 2026 describes a bidirectional relationship: periodontal disease is more severe and possibly more prevalent in diabetes and is associated with higher A1C; people with periodontal disease have higher rates of incident diabetes; periodontal treatment may improve glycaemia; and people with diabetes should have a dental exam at least yearly.
version: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026; Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S61-S88 (Section 4) and S27-S49 (Section 2)
document: 4. Comprehensive Medical Evaluation and Assessment of Comorbidities: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Section 4 'Dental Care', Rec 4.15; Section 2 screening text
quote: Periodontal disease is more severe, and may be more prevalent, in people with diabetes than in those without ... Longitudinal studies suggest that people with periodontal disease have higher rates of incident diabetes ... People with diabetes should be referred for a dental exam at least once per year

topic: IDF Diabetes Atlas: Uganda adult diabetes numbers
claim: The IDF member page for Uganda (2024 data) lists an adult population of 22,022,200, a diabetes prevalence in adults of 2.2% and 369,100 adults with diabetes.
version: IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th edition (2025), 2024 estimates as shown on idf.org
document: IDF Africa members: Uganda (country page)
quote: "Total adult population" - "22,022,200" ... "Prevalence of diabetes in adults" - "2.2%" ... "Total cases of diabetes in adults" - "369,100"
conflicts: 369,100 / 22,022,200 = 1.7%, not 2.2%; the 2.2% shown is therefore probably the age-standardised (comparative) prevalence while the count reflects crude prevalence - the page gives no footnote. Uganda STEPS 2014 measured 1.4% (18-69 y, fasting capillary).

topic: IDF Diabetes Atlas: Africa region undiagnosed proportion and projection
claim: IDF Atlas 11th edition regional figures for Africa (adults with diabetes in 2024, projection to 2050, proportion undiagnosed) could not be opened; values below are from memory and unverified.
document: IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th edition
quote: 589 million adults (20-79 years) are living with diabetes – 1 in 9

claim: The 2014 Uganda STEPS survey (3987 adults aged 18-69) found raised fasting blood glucose in 1.4% (0.9-1.9) and impaired fasting glycaemia in 2.0% (1.5-2.5), measured on fasting capillary whole blood.
document: 2014 STEPS Fact Sheet Uganda
section: Step 3 Biochemical Measurement; Step 2 Physical Measurements
quote: A total of 3987 adults participated in the survey. ... Percentage with raised fasting blood glucose ... capillary whole blood value ≥ 7.0 mmol/L (≥126 mg/dl): 1.4 (0.9-1.9) | 1.6 (0.8-2.6) | 1.1 (0.6-1.7)
conflicts: The WHO fact-sheet footnote as relayed applies the 7.0 mmol/L threshold to capillary whole blood; WHO 2006 fasting thresholds for venous plasma and capillary are the same (7.0), but meters differ in plasma-calibration - the survey device/calibration was not checked here.

claim: In the 2014 national survey, 48.9% of Ugandans found to have diabetes and 90.5% of those with impaired fasting glycaemia were not aware of their hyperglycaemia; diabetes prevalence was 2.7% urban vs 1.0% rural.
document: Prevalence and correlates of diabetes mellitus in Uganda: a population-based national survey (Bahendeka S, Wesonga R, Mutungi G, Muwonge J, Neema S, Guwatudde D)
quote: The overall prevalence of IFG was 2.0% (95% confidence interval (CI) = 1.5-2.5%), whereas that of diabetes was 1.4% (95% CI 0.9-1.9%). ... The majority of participants identified with hyperglycaemia (90.5% of IFG and 48.9% of diabetes) were not aware of their hyperglycaemic status.

claim: The Uganda STEPS 2023 report (3,694 adults aged 18-69, response rate 86%) states that risk factors changed little from 2014 but increased in some instances, naming hyperglycaemia; the actual 2023 prevalence figure could not be read.
version: Uganda NCD Risk Factors STEPS Survey 2023 report (MoH/WHO)
document: 2023 STEPS Country Report Uganda
quote: The number of participants enrolled into the Non-communicable Disease Risk Factors STEPS survey Uganda 2023 was 3,694 (1,426 men; 2,268 women), giving a response rate of 86%. ... findings point to significant risk factors in the population and with little change from the previous STEPS survey of 2014; and in some instances, an increase as in hyperglycaemia

topic: Systematic review: diabetes risk tools in sub-Saharan Africa
claim: A 2022 systematic review of 39 articles concluded that no available diabetes risk assessment tool had been developed and validated for the sub-Saharan African population, and that studies used FINDRISC without local validation.
document: A systematic review of diabetes risk assessment tools in sub-Saharan Africa (Ekure E, Ovenseri-Ogbomo G, Osuagwu UL, et al.)
quote: Of the 825 articles identified, 39 articles met the inclusion criteria ... This comprehensive review of the available literature found that no available diabetes risk assessment tool was developed and validated for the SSA population
conflicts: Contradicts the existence of the ADRS (Mayige 2014 thesis, derived in Tanzania/Senegal/Guinea and validated in South Africa/Guinea/Tanzania): the review did not mention ADRS or Mayige, presumably because the derivation is a thesis rather than an indexed journal article. Royce 2024 calls ADRS 'the only prediction model that has been developed in a sub-Saharan African population'.

topic: Stress hyperglycaemia is not diagnostic of diabetes (WHO)
claim: WHO states that severe hyperglycaemia found during acute infective, traumatic, circulatory or other stress may be transitory and should not in itself be regarded as diagnostic of diabetes.
document: Definition, Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes Mellitus and its Complications. Report of a WHO Consultation. Part 1: Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes Mellitus
quote: Severe hyperglycaemia detected under conditions of acute infective, traumatic, circulatory or other stress may be transitory and should not in itself be regarded as diagnostic of diabetes.
conflicts: WHO gives no retest interval. NICE NG185 (post-ACS) is the only source found with a time rule: fasting glucose no earlier than 4 days after onset, plus HbA1c before discharge. ADA 2026 uses admission A1C >= 6.5% to infer pre-existing diabetes rather than waiting.

topic: Asymptomatic person: never diagnose on a single abnormal glucose (WHO)
claim: WHO states the diagnosis of diabetes in an asymptomatic subject should never be made on the basis of a single abnormal blood glucose value.
document: Definition, Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes Mellitus and its Complications. Report of a WHO Consultation. Part 1: Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes Mellitus
quote: The diagnosis of diabetes in an asymptomatic subject should never be made on the basis of a single abnormal blood glucose value.
conflicts: ADA 2026 allows confirmation by two different abnormal tests from the same sample: 'two abnormal screening test results, measured either at the same time or at two different time points'. WHO requires a further glucose test.

claim: WHO specifies the OGTT in the morning after at least three days of unrestricted diet (> 150 g carbohydrate daily) and usual activity, after an overnight fast of 8-14 hours, with no smoking, using 75 g anhydrous glucose in 250-300 ml water drunk over 5 minutes and a blood sample at 2 hours.
document: Definition, Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes Mellitus and its Complications. Report of a WHO Consultation. Part 1: Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes Mellitus
quote: The OGTT should be administered in the morning after at least three days of unrestricted diet (greater than 150 g of carbohydrate daily) and usual physical activity ... preceded by an overnight fast of 8-14 hours ... Smoking is not permitted ... 75 g of anhydrous glucose ... in 250-300 ml of water over the course of 5 minutes
conflicts: ADA/ADLM define fasting as 'at least 8 h' with no upper limit; WHO gives 8-14 hours. ADA 2026 words the carbohydrate requirement as 'at least 150 g/day'.

claim: WHO 1999 said that unless glucose can be measured immediately, blood should be collected into a sodium fluoride tube, centrifuged immediately to separate plasma, and the plasma frozen.
document: Definition, Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes Mellitus and its Complications. Report of a WHO Consultation. Part 1: Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes Mellitus
quote: Unless the glucose concentration can be determined immediately, the blood sample should be collected in a tube containing sodium fluoride ... and immediately centrifuged to separate the plasma; the plasma should be frozen.
conflicts: ADLM/ADA 2023: 'Tubes with only enolase inhibitors such as sodium fluoride should not be relied on to prevent glycolysis' and prefers citrate buffer or ice-slurry with centrifugation within 15-30 min. Both agree that prompt separation is essential; they differ on whether fluoride is adequate.

topic: ADA: confirmation of diagnosis and near-threshold results
claim: ADA 2026 requires confirmatory testing unless there is unequivocal hyperglycaemia; confirmation can be two abnormal results from the same sample or different times, and results near the threshold should be repeated in 3-6 months.
version: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026; Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S27-S49
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia (e.g., hyperglycemic crises), diagnosis requires confirmatory testing ... This can be accomplished by two abnormal screening test results, measured either at the same time or at two different time points. ... Test results close to the diagnostic threshold should prompt the health care professional ... to repeat the test in 3–6 months.

claim: WHO/IDF 2006 keeps the diagnostic criteria for diabetes at fasting plasma glucose >= 7.0 mmol/L or 2-h plasma glucose >= 11.1 mmol/L.
document: Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycaemia: report of a WHO/IDF consultation
section: Summary of Technical Report and recommendations, Recommendation 1 (p.1) and summary table
quote: Recommendation 1 The current WHO diagnostic criteria for diabetes should be maintained – fasting plasma glucose ≥ 7.0mmol/l (126mg/dl) or 2–h plasma glucose ≥ 11.1mmol/l (200mg/dl).
conflicts: ADA uses the same FPG and 2-h values; ADA also lists HbA1c >= 6.5% and random >= 11.1 with symptoms in one table (WHO added HbA1c only in 2011).

claim: HEARTS-D Table 3 gives the WHO diagnostic cut-offs for primary care, including a separate 2-hour capillary value and a random value usable only with symptoms.
document: Diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes (HEARTS-D)
section: Section 'Diagnostic tests', Table 3 'Diagnostic criteria for diabetes' (p.13)
quote: Fasting venous or capillary plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) | 2-hour post-load venous plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) | 2-hour post-load capillary plasma glucose ≥12.2 mmol/L (220 mg/dL) | Random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) To be used only in the presence of symptoms | HbA1c 6.5% (48 mmol/mol)
conflicts: ADA has no separate capillary 2-h threshold and does not accept capillary/point-of-care glucose for diagnosis; ADA diagnostic values otherwise identical.

claim: WHO 2019 states all four diagnostic routes in one sentence, with random glucose requiring signs and symptoms.
document: Classification of diabetes mellitus
quote: People with fasting plasma glucose values of ≥ 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dl), 2-h post-load plasma glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dl) (5), HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (48 mmol/mol); or a random blood glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dl) in the presence of signs and symptoms are considered to have diabetes

claim: In asymptomatic people a single abnormal result is not enough: repeat, preferably the same test, on a subsequent day.
document: Diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes (HEARTS-D)
section: Section 'Diagnostic tests' (p.13); Fig. 1 box 'IF ASYMPTOMATIC repeat test on subsequent day'
quote: In asymptomatic people, repeat the test to confirm the diagnosis, preferably with the same test, as soon as practicable on a subsequent day.
conflicts: ADA: two abnormal results needed (same sample with two different tests, or two samples) unless unequivocal hyperglycaemia/hyperglycaemic crisis - ADA allows two different tests on the SAME sample, which WHO does not mention.

claim: WHO 2011: an asymptomatic person must not be diagnosed on one abnormal glucose or HbA1c value; one further diabetic-range result is required.
document: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus: Abbreviated Report of a WHO Consultation
section: Chapter 2, Glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) for the diagnosis of diabetes
quote: The diagnosis of diabetes in an asymptomatic person should not be made on the basis of a single abnormal plasma glucose or HbA1c value. At least one additional HbA1c or plasma glucose test result with a value in the diabetic range is required, either fasting, from a random (casual) sample, or from the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT).

claim: WHO 2011 accepts HbA1c >= 6.5% as a diagnostic test under quality conditions; a value below 6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed by glucose tests.
document: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus: Abbreviated Report of a WHO Consultation
quote: HbA1c can be used as a diagnostic test for diabetes providing that stringent quality assurance tests are in place and assays are standardised to criteria aligned to the international reference values [...] An HbA1c of 6.5% is recommended as the cut point for diagnosing diabetes. A value of less than 6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed using glucose tests.
conflicts: ADA gives the same 6.5% threshold but requires an NGSP-certified, DCCT-standardised laboratory method (not point-of-care unless FDA-cleared for diagnosis).

claim: WHO made no formal recommendation on interpreting HbA1c below 6.5% (no WHO HbA1c 'prediabetes' range).
document: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus: Abbreviated Report of a WHO Consultation
quote: Levels of HbA1c just below 6.5% may indicate the presence of intermediate hyperglycaemia. The precise lower cut-off point for this has yet to be defined, although the ADA has suggested 5.7 – 6.4% as the high risk range. The consultation concluded that there is insufficient evidence to make any formal recommendation on the interpretation of HbA1c levels below 6.5%.
conflicts: ADA defines prediabetes as HbA1c 5.7-6.4% (39-47 mmol/mol); the International Expert Committee/NICE use 6.0-6.4% (42-47 mmol/mol). WHO defines no HbA1c intermediate category.

claim: WHO lists haemoglobinopathies, certain anaemias and malaria among the main factors distorting HbA1c; Annex 1 adds iron/B12 deficiency, renal failure and antiretrovirals.
document: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus: Abbreviated Report of a WHO Consultation
section: Chapter 2 and Annex 1 'Some of the factors that influence HbA1c and its measurement' (NBK304266)
quote: HbA1c may be affected by a variety of genetic, haematologic and illness-related factors. The most common important factors worldwide affecting HbA1c levels are haemoglobinopathies (depending on the assay employed), certain anaemias, and disorders associated with accelerated red cell turnover such as malaria.

claim: WHO defines IGT as fasting plasma glucose < 7.0 mmol/L AND 2-h plasma glucose >= 7.8 and < 11.1 mmol/L.
document: Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycaemia: report of a WHO/IDF consultation
section: Summary table of diagnostic criteria (p.1); Recommendation 3
quote: Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) Fasting plasma glucose 2–h plasma glucose* <7.0mmol/l (126mg/dl) and ≥7.8 and <11.1mmol/l (140mg/dl and 200mg/dl)
conflicts: ADA IGT: 2-h 7.8-11.0 mmol/L (140-199 mg/dL) - same range.

claim: WHO defines IFG as fasting plasma glucose 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L and (if measured) 2-h plasma glucose < 7.8 mmol/L.
document: Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycaemia: report of a WHO/IDF consultation
quote: Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) Fasting plasma glucose 2–h plasma glucose* 6.1 to 6.9mmol/l (110mg/dl to 125mg/dl) and (if measured) <7.8mmol/l (140mg/dl) [...] If 2–h plasma glucose is not measured, status is uncertain as diabetes or IGT cannot be excluded
conflicts: CONFLICT: ADA IFG = 5.6-6.9 mmol/L (100-125 mg/dL); WHO IFG = 6.1-6.9 mmol/L (110-125 mg/dL). A fasting value of 5.6-6.0 mmol/L is 'prediabetes' under ADA but normal under WHO.

claim: WHO kept the IFG cut-point at 6.1 mmol/L because lowering it to 5.6 would sharply raise prevalence without evidence of benefit.
document: Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycaemia: report of a WHO/IDF consultation
section: Summary of Technical Report and recommendations, Recommendation 4 (p.1)
quote: Recommendation 4 The fasting plasma glucose cut-point for Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) should remain at 6.1mmol/l. This decision was based on concerns about the significant increase in IFG prevalence which would occur with lowering the cut-point and the impact on individuals and health systems.
conflicts: CONFLICT: ADA lowered the IFG threshold to 5.6 mmol/L in 2003; WHO explicitly declined.

claim: WHO retains the OGTT and says people with fasting plasma glucose 6.1-6.9 mmol/L should have an OGTT to determine glucose tolerance status.
document: Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycaemia: report of a WHO/IDF consultation
quote: An OGTT should be used in individuals with fasting plasma glucose 6.1–6.9mmol/l (110–125mg/dl) to determine glucose tolerance status.
conflicts: ADA does not mandate an OGTT for IFG; it accepts FPG, 2-h OGTT or HbA1c interchangeably.

claim: Venous plasma is the WHO standard; fasting capillary and venous plasma values are identical, but the 2-hour post-load capillary diagnostic value is higher (12.2 mmol/L).
document: Diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes (HEARTS-D)
quote: Venous plasma glucose is the standard method for measuring and reporting. However, in recognition of the widespread use of capillary sampling, especially in low-resource settings, values for capillary plasma glucose are provided for post-load glucose values. Fasting values for venous and capillary plasma glucose are identical.
conflicts: ADA: point-of-care/capillary glucose should not be used for diagnosis. WHO explicitly permits it in low-resource settings.

claim: HEARTS-D allows point-of-care devices when no laboratory is available, and urine glucose only to support suspicion in symptomatic people.
document: Diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes (HEARTS-D)
quote: If laboratory measurement is not available, point of care, ("finger stick") devices can be used (they report glucose values in capillary plasma). | If plasma glucose measurement is not possible, urine glucose testing can be used to confirm suspicion of diabetes in people with symptoms. A negative urine test does not exclude diabetes, but it excludes severe hyperglycaemia.

claim: WHO 2019 classifies diabetes into type 1, type 2, hybrid forms, other specific types, unclassified diabetes, and hyperglycaemia first detected during pregnancy.
document: Classification of diabetes mellitus
quote: Type 1 diabetes / Type 2 diabetes / Hybrid forms of diabetes / Slowly evolving immune-mediated diabetes of adults / Ketosis prone type 2 diabetes / Other specific types (see Tables) / Monogenic diabetes / [...] / Unclassified diabetes / Hyperglyacemia first detected during pregnancy / Diabetes mellitus in pregnancy / Gestational diabetes mellitus
conflicts: ADA keeps four classes (type 1 incl. LADA; type 2; specific types due to other causes; gestational diabetes) and has no 'hybrid' or 'unclassified' category - ADA treats LADA as type 1.

claim: 'Unclassified diabetes' is a temporary label for use near diagnosis when the type is not yet clear; efforts to classify should continue.
document: Classification of diabetes mellitus
quote: This category should be used temporarily when there is not a clear diagnostic category especially close to the time of diagnosis of diabetes [...] Until there is a definite diagnosis of the type of diabetes, a classification of 'unclassified' should be used and attempts to classify the type of diabetes should continue to support appropriate management decisions.
conflicts: ADA has no equivalent category.

claim: Slowly evolving immune-mediated diabetes of adults has no agreed criteria; three are commonly used (GAD antibody positive, age > 35 at diagnosis, no insulin needed for 6-12 months).
document: Classification of diabetes mellitus
quote: There are no universally agreed criteria for this subtype of diabetes, but three criteria are often used: positivity for GAD autoantibodies, age older than 35 years at diagnosis, and no need for insulin therapy in the first 6–12 months after diagnosis
conflicts: ADA classifies LADA under type 1 diabetes; WHO places it under 'hybrid forms'.

claim: Ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes presents with ketosis and severe insulin deficiency but later remits off insulin; it is described in sub-Saharan African populations.
document: Classification of diabetes mellitus
section: Hybrid forms of diabetes: ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes (pp.16-17)
quote: Subsequently similar phenotypes were described in populations in sub-Saharan African. Typically, those affected present with ketosis and evidence of severe insulin deficiency but later go into remission and do not require insulin treatment. Reports suggest that further ketotic episodes occur in 90% of these people within 10 years.
conflicts: ADA mentions ketosis-prone ('Flatbush') diabetes under type 2/idiopathic type 1 rather than as a separate hybrid form.

claim: WHO gives five steps for clinically subtyping a newly diagnosed person, relying on clinical features where antibodies and C-peptide are unavailable.

claim: A single random plasma glucose >=200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) with classic symptoms or a hyperglycaemic crisis is a clear clinical diagnosis and needs no confirmatory test.
