quote: In the absence of a clear clinical diagnosis (e.g., individual with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis and random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL [≥11.1 mmol/L]), confirmatory tests are necessary to establish the diagnosis. This can be accomplished by two abnormal screening test results, measured either at the same time or at two different time points.

claim: 'Random' means any time of day regardless of the last meal; classic symptoms are polyuria, polydipsia and unexplained weight loss.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Table 2.1, fourth row (random plasma glucose criterion); diagnostic narrative
quote: Random is any time of the day without regard to time since previous meal.

claim: ADA defines prediabetes by A1C 5.7-6.4%, IFG (FPG 100-125 mg/dL) or IGT (2-h PG 140-199 mg/dL).
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Table 2.2 (Criteria defining prediabetes in nonpregnant individuals)
quote: A1C 5.7–6.4% (39–47 mmol/mol) [...] FPG 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) to 125 mg/dL (6.9 mmol/L) (IFG) [...] 2-h PG during 75-g OGTT 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) to 199 mg/dL (11.0 mmol/L) (IGT)
conflicts: WHO (and several other organisations) set the IFG lower limit at 110 mg/dL (6.1 mmol/L) - ADA says so itself (next item). WHO does not use an A1C range for intermediate hyperglycaemia (WHO side to be confirmed in the WHO-domain dossier).

claim: ADA explicitly notes that WHO and several diabetes organisations define the IFG lower limit at 110 mg/dL (6.1 mmol/L), not ADA's 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L).
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: IFG is defined as FPG levels from 100 to 125 mg/dL (from 5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L) and IGT as 2-h PG levels during 75-g OGTT from 140 to 199 mg/dL (from 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L). It should be noted that the World Health Organization and several diabetes organizations define the IFG lower limit at 110 mg/dL (6.1 mmol/L).
conflicts: ADA IFG 5.6-6.9 mmol/L vs WHO IFG 6.1-6.9 mmol/L. The engine must label which standard a 'prediabetes/IFG' flag follows; Uganda Clinical Guidelines follow WHO.

claim: If two different tests disagree, repeat the test that was above the diagnostic cut point; the diagnosis is made on the confirmed test, even if the other test stays below threshold.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: if an individual has discordant results from two different tests, then the test result that is above the diagnostic cut point should be repeated, with careful consideration of factors that may affect measured A1C or glucose levels. The diagnosis is made based on the confirmatory screening test.

claim: Results close to the diagnostic threshold should prompt education about symptoms and a repeat test in 3-6 months.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Test results close to the diagnostic threshold should prompt the health care professional to educate the individual about the onset of possible symptoms of hyperglycemia and to repeat the test in 3–6 months.

claim: Consistent, substantial discordance between glucose and A1C should trigger a search for an assay problem or interference; fructosamine or glycated albumin are the alternative markers for monitoring.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Evaluate for the possibility of a problem or interference with either test when there is consistent and substantial discordance between blood glucose values and A1C test results.

claim: Where the A1C-glycaemia relationship is altered (some haemoglobin variants, pregnancy, G6PD deficiency, HIV, altered red-cell turnover), use plasma glucose criteria to diagnose diabetes.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: In conditions associated with an altered relationship between A1C and glycemia, such as some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, HIV, and conditions that may alter red blood cell turnover, plasma glucose criteria should be used to diagnose diabetes.

claim: Table 2.3 lists the individual factors that alter A1C: altered erythrocyte turnover (anaemia, iron status, splenectomy, blood loss, transfusion, haemolysis, G6PD deficiency, erythropoietin), HIV, cirrhosis, kidney failure, dialysis, pregnancy; and assay interferences (haemoglobin variants, severe hypertriglyceridaemia, severe hyperbilirubinaemia).
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Table 2.3 (Considerations related to use and interpretation of laboratory measurements of glucose and A1C)
quote: Altered erythrocyte turnover (e.g., anemia, iron status, splenectomy, blood loss, transfusion, hemolysis, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, erythropoietin), HIV, cirrhosis, kidney failure, dialysis, pregnancy

claim: A1C may not be a suitable diagnostic test in anaemia, erythropoietin treatment, haemodialysis or HIV treatment; factors affecting haemoglobin or erythrocyte turnover (e.g. thalassaemia, folate deficiency) alter A1C.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Narrative 'Use of A1C for Screening and Diagnosis of Diabetes'
quote: A1C may not be a suitable diagnostic test in people with anemia, people treated with erythropoietin, or people undergoing hemodialysis or HIV treatment.

claim: In sickle cell trait an A1C assay free of haemoglobin-variant interference must be used; the G6PD G202A variant (11% of Black individuals in the U.S.) lowers A1C by about 0.8% (homozygous men) / 0.7% (homozygous women).
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Narrative 'Use of A1C for Screening and Diagnosis of Diabetes'
quote: Some A1C assays can be affected by hemoglobin variants. For instance, an A1C assay without interference from hemoglobin variants should be used in individuals with sickle cell trait. [...] glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase G202A, carried by 11% of Black individuals in the U.S., is associated with a decrease in A1C of about 0.8% in homozygous men and 0.7% in homozygous women

claim: A1C for diagnosis must be measured by an NGSP-certified method traceable to the DCCT reference assay.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: The A1C test should be performed using a method that is certified by the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP) as traceable to the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) reference assay.

claim: Point-of-care A1C may be used for screening/diagnosis only with devices FDA-approved for diagnosis, in CLIA-certified laboratories of moderate complexity or higher, by trained personnel.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Point-of-care A1C testing for diabetes screening and diagnosis should be restricted to devices approved for diagnosis by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration at Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments–certified laboratories that perform testing of moderate complexity or higher by trained personnel.

claim: ADA diagnostic criteria are stated on plasma glucose; glucose measurement varies by sample type (plasma, serum, whole blood) and source (capillary, venous, arterial), and samples must be separated immediately or kept on ice to prevent glycolysis.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Table 2.3; narrative 'Use of Fasting Plasma Glucose or 2-Hour Plasma Glucose for Screening and Diagnosis of Diabetes'
quote: Poor; plasma must be separated immediately or samples must be kept on ice to prevent glycolysis [...] Measurement can vary depending on sample type (plasma, serum, whole blood) and source (capillary, venous, arterial) [...] Glucose concentrations will be falsely low if samples are not processed and analyzed promptly.
conflicts: WHO (2006 diagnostic report; WHO PEN/HEARTS) explicitly allows capillary glucose where laboratory venous plasma is unavailable (fasting values identical, 2-h capillary threshold higher) - to be confirmed from the WHO-domain dossier. ADA Section 2 gives no such allowance.

claim: There is insufficient evidence to use continuous glucose monitoring for screening or diagnosis of prediabetes or diabetes.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: There is presently insufficient evidence to support the use of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) for screening or diagnosis of prediabetes or diabetes.

claim: Before an OGTT, adequate carbohydrate intake (at least 150 g/day) should be assured for the 3 preceding days.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: When using OGTT as a screening tool for prediabetes or diabetes, adequate carbohydrate intake (at least 150 g/day) should be assured for 3 days prior to testing.

claim: The 2-h PG identifies more people with prediabetes and diabetes than FPG or A1C cut points, and is preferentially recommended for cystic-fibrosis-related diabetes and post-transplantation diabetes screening; A1C has lower sensitivity at its cut point.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Narrative 'Use of Fasting Plasma Glucose or 2-Hour Plasma Glucose...' and 'Use of A1C...'
quote: the 2-h PG (OGTT) testing protocol is significantly more sensitive than the other two tests and is preferentially recommended for screening for some conditions (e.g., cystic fibrosis–related diabetes or posttransplantation diabetes mellitus).

claim: ADA 2026 Section 2 does not adopt, and (in the text read) does not mention, the IDF 1-hour 75-g OGTT criteria; a 1-h value is used only inside the GDM tables.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Section 2 narrative (searched: 'Screening and Diagnosis of Diabetes', 'Use of Fasting Plasma Glucose or 2-Hour Plasma Glucose...', 'Use of A1C...', 'Confirming the Diagnosis', 'Prediabetes and Type 2 Diabetes')
quote: Diabetes may be diagnosed based on A1C or plasma glucose criteria. Plasma glucose criteria include either the fasting plasma glucose (FPG), 2-h plasma glucose (2-h PG) during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), or random glucose accompanied by classic symptoms
conflicts: IDF Position Statement 2024 proposes 1-h PG >=155 mg/dL (8.6 mmol/L) for intermediate hyperglycaemia and >=209 mg/dL (11.6 mmol/L) for type 2 diabetes (IDF values from memory - NOT verified here; to be sourced from the IDF document). ADA has not incorporated them.

claim: Screen asymptomatic adults by risk assessment; test adults of any age with overweight/obesity plus >=1 risk factor; otherwise start at age 35; repeat at least every 3 years if normal.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Testing for prediabetes or type 2 diabetes in asymptomatic people should be considered in adults of any age with overweight or obesity who have one or more risk factors (Table 2.5). B [...] For all other people, screening should begin at age 35 years. B [...] repeat screening recommended at a minimum of 3-year intervals is reasonable, sooner with symptoms or change in risk (e.g., weight gain). C
conflicts: WHO PEN / Uganda Clinical Guidelines use different (generally age >=40 or symptom/risk-based) screening triggers - to be taken from those dossiers.

claim: Table 2.5: consider testing adults with BMI >=25 kg/m2 (>=23 kg/m2 in individuals of Asian ancestry) who have one or more listed risk factors.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Table 2.5 (Criteria for screening for diabetes or prediabetes in asymptomatic adults), item 1
quote: Testing should be considered in adults with overweight or obesity (BMI ≥25 kg/m2 or ≥23 kg/m2 in individuals of Asian ancestry) who have one or more of the following risk factors: First-degree relative with diabetes [...] Hypertension (≥130/80 mmHg or on therapy for hypertension) [...] HDL cholesterol level <35 mg/dL (<0.9 mmol/L) and/or triglyceride level >250 mg/dL (>2.8 mmol/L)

claim: Table 2.5: prediabetes - test yearly; prior GDM - test at least every 1-3 years; everyone else from age 35; repeat at minimum 3-yearly if normal; other high-risk groups (HIV, high-risk medicines, periodontal disease, history of pancreatitis) closely monitored.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: People with prediabetes (A1C ≥5.7% [≥39 mmol/mol], IGT, or IFG) should be tested yearly. [...] People who were diagnosed with GDM should have testing at least every 1–3 years. [...] Individuals in other high-risk groups (e.g., people with HIV, exposure to high-risk medicines, evidence of periodontal disease, history of pancreatitis) should also be closely monitored.

claim: FPG, 2-h PG during 75-g OGTT and A1C are each appropriate screening tests for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: To screen for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes, FPG, 2-h PG during 75-g OGTT, and A1C are each appropriate (Table 2.1 and Table 2.2).

claim: Screening should ideally occur within a health-care setting; community screening outside health care is generally not recommended.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Community screening outside a health care setting is generally not recommended because people with positive tests may not seek, or have access to, appropriate follow-up testing and care.

claim: People with HIV: screen with fasting plasma glucose before starting ART, when switching ART, and 3-6 months after starting or switching; if normal, check FPG annually.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: People with HIV should be screened for diabetes and prediabetes with an FPG test before starting antiretroviral therapy, at the time of switching antiretroviral therapy, and 3–6 months after starting or switching antiretroviral therapy. If initial screening results are normal, FPG should be checked annually.

claim: A1C may underestimate glycaemia in people with HIV, so plasma glucose criteria are preferred; risk is increased with certain protease inhibitors and NRTIs.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: As the A1C test may underestimate glycemia in people with HIV, plasma glucose criteria are preferred to diagnose prediabetes and diabetes. [...] Diabetes risk is increased with certain protease inhibitors (PIs) and nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs).

claim: Consider screening people on statins, thiazide diuretics and some HIV medications; with second-generation antipsychotics screen at baseline, 12-16 weeks after initiation, then annually.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Consider screening people for prediabetes or diabetes if they are on certain medications, such as statins, thiazide diuretics, and some HIV medications, as these agents are known to increase the risk of these conditions.

claim: With recurrent or long-term glucocorticoid use, monitor postprandial or random glucose (not fasting).
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Monitor postprandial or random glucose levels with recurrent or long-term use of glucocorticoids.

claim: People starting immune checkpoint inhibitors, PI3K-alpha inhibitors or mTOR inhibitors need education on hyperglycaemia/crises and scheduled glucose testing; ICI-induced autoimmune diabetes occurs in 0.6-1.4% and often presents as DKA.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Recommendations 2.19-2.22; narrative 'Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-Induced Autoimmune Diabetes'
quote: ICI-induced autoimmune diabetes occurs in 0.6–1.4% of treated people, often presents as DKA, and almost invariably requires lifelong insulin therapy.

claim: Pancreatic (pancreatogenic / type 3c) diabetes is commonly misdiagnosed as type 2; screen within 3-6 months after acute pancreatitis and annually thereafter, and annually in chronic pancreatitis.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Recommendation 2.23; narrative 'Pancreatic Diabetes or Diabetes in the Context of Disease of the Exocrine Pancreas'
quote: Screen people for diabetes within 3–6 months following an episode of acute pancreatitis and annually thereafter. Screening for diabetes is recommended annually for people with chronic pancreatitis.

claim: Risk-based screening in youth: after onset of puberty or age 10 (whichever is earlier) in those with overweight (BMI >=85th percentile) or obesity (>=95th) plus >=1 risk factor; repeat at minimum 3-yearly.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Recommendation 2.15; Table 2.6 (Risk-based screening for type 2 diabetes or prediabetes in asymptomatic children and adolescents in a clinical setting)
quote: Risk-based screening for prediabetes or type 2 diabetes should be considered after the onset of puberty or after 10 years of age, whichever occurs earlier, in children and adolescents with overweight (BMI ≥ 85th percentile) or obesity (BMI ≥ 95th percentile) and who have one or more risk factors for diabetes.

claim: ADA classifies diabetes into type 1 (including LADA), type 2, specific types due to other causes, and gestational diabetes mellitus.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: 1. Type 1 diabetes (due to autoimmune β-cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency, including latent autoimmune diabetes in adults) 2. Type 2 diabetes (due to a nonautoimmune progressive loss of adequate β-cell insulin secretion, frequently on the background of insulin resistance) 3. Specific types of diabetes due to other causes
conflicts: WHO 2019 classification adds 'hybrid forms' (slowly evolving immune-mediated diabetes; ketosis-prone type 2) and 'unclassified' as separate categories - WHO side to be confirmed in the WHO-domain dossier.

claim: The AABBCC approach (Age, Autoimmunity, Body habitus, Background, Control, Comorbidities) helps distinguish type 1 from type 2 diabetes; it is not prospectively validated.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Although not prospectively validated, the AABBCC approach is a useful tool to help distinguish type 1 from type 2 diabetes: Age (e.g., for individuals <35 years old, consider type 1 diabetes); Autoimmunity (e.g., personal or family history of autoimmune disease or polyglandular autoimmune syndromes); Body habitus (e.g., BMI <25 kg/m2); Background (e.g., family history of type 1 diabetes);

claim: Standardised islet autoantibody tests are recommended to classify diabetes in adults with features overlapping type 1; GAD first, then IA-2 and/or ZnT8; 5-10% of type 1 is antibody-negative.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Standardized islet autoantibody tests are recommended for classification of diabetes in adults who have phenotypic risk factors that overlap with those for type 1 diabetes (e.g., younger age at diagnosis, unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, or short time to insulin treatment).

claim: C-peptide is indicated only in insulin-treated people; a random sample with concurrent glucose within 5 h of eating suffices. >=600 pmol/L needs no qualification; <600 with glucose <4 mmol/L or fasting - consider repeating; <80 pmol/L need not be repeated; 200-600 pmol/L usually type 1 or MODY.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Figure 2.1 footnotes 4 and 9 (flowchart for investigation of suspected type 1 diabetes in newly diagnosed adults)
quote: If the result is ≥600 pmol/L (≥1.8 ng/mL), the circumstances of testing do not matter. If the result is <600 pmol/L (<1.8 ng/mL) and the concurrent glucose is <4 mmol/L (<70 mg/dL) or the person may have been fasting, consider repeating the test. Results showing very low levels (e.g., <80 pmol/L [<0.24 ng/mL]) do not need to be repeated.

claim: Type 1 diabetes is staged 1-3: stage 1 multiple autoantibodies with normoglycaemia; stage 2 autoantibodies with dysglycaemia; stage 3 overt hyperglycaemia meeting standard diabetes criteria.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Islet autoantibodies (usually multiple) Dysglycemia: IFG: FPG 100–125 mg/dL (5.6–6.9 mmol/L) or IGT: 2-h PG 140–199 mg/dL (7.8–11.0 mmol/L) or A1C 5.7–6.4% (39–47 mmol/mol) or ≥10% increase in A1C

claim: Presymptomatic type 1 screening uses islet autoantibodies (insulin, GAD, IA-2, ZnT8), offered to those with a family history or known genetic risk; multiple confirmed antibodies warrant specialist referral and consideration of teplizumab or trials.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Individuals with multiple confirmed islet autoantibodies and without overt type 1 diabetes have a high risk for progression to stage 3 type 1 diabetes and should be referred to a specialized center for metabolic staging (Table 2.4), education, and consideration of prevention trials or approved treatments (e.g., teplizumab).

claim: Monogenic diabetes (MODY) is suggested by A1C <58 mmol/mol (<7.5%) at diagnosis, one parent with diabetes, features of a specific monogenic cause, or MODY-calculator probability >5%.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Monogenic diabetes is suggested by the presence of one or more of the following features: A1C <58 mmol/mol (<7.5%) at diagnosis, one parent with diabetes, features of a specific monogenic cause (e.g., renal cysts, partial lipodystrophy, maternally inherited deafness, and severe insulin resistance in the absence of obesity), and monogenic diabetes prediction model probability >5%

claim: People with type 2 diabetes may occasionally present with DKA (ketosis-prone diabetes), particularly Black and Hispanic/Latino adults.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Occasionally, people with type 2 diabetes may present with DKA (33) in the context of ketosis-prone diabetes, particularly members of certain racial, ethnic, and ancestral groups (e.g., Black and Hispanic/Latino adults) (27).
conflicts: WHO 2019 classifies 'ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes' as a distinct hybrid form; ADA keeps it inside type 2 (WHO side to be confirmed in WHO-domain dossier).

claim: ADA places all autoimmune beta-cell destruction, whatever the age of onset, under type 1 diabetes; 'LADA' is an acceptable clinical term. Idiopathic type 1 is insulinopenic and DKA-prone without autoimmunity.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: For this classification, all forms of diabetes mediated by autoimmune β-cell destruction independent of age of onset are included under the rubric of type 1 diabetes. Use of the term LADA is common and acceptable in clinical practice
conflicts: WHO 2019 lists 'slowly evolving immune-mediated diabetes of adults' as a hybrid form rather than type 1 (WHO side to be confirmed).

claim: GDM one-step strategy: 75-g OGTT at 24-28 weeks; GDM if any value met or exceeded - fasting 92 mg/dL, 1 h 180 mg/dL, 2 h 153 mg/dL.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Table 2.8 (Screening for and diagnosis of GDM), one-step strategy
quote: Perform a 75-g OGTT, with plasma glucose measurement when fasting and at 1 and 2 h, at 24–28 weeks of gestation in individuals not previously diagnosed with diabetes. [...] The diagnosis of GDM is made when any of the following plasma glucose values are met or exceeded: Fasting: 92 mg/dL (5.1 mmol/L) 1 h: 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) 2 h: 153 mg/dL (8.5 mmol/L)
conflicts: Same thresholds as WHO 2013 'gestational diabetes mellitus' (which derive from IADPSG 2010); WHO additionally defines 'diabetes in pregnancy' by non-pregnant criteria (WHO side to be confirmed).

claim: GDM two-step strategy: 50-g non-fasting GLT at 24-28 weeks; if 1-h >=130, 135 or 140 mg/dL proceed to fasting 100-g OGTT; GDM if at least two of four Carpenter-Coustan values are met or exceeded.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Table 2.8 (Screening for and diagnosis of GDM), two-step strategy
quote: If the plasma glucose level measured 1 h after the load is ≥130, 135, or 140 mg/dL (7.2, 7.5, or 7.8 mmol/L, respectively),* proceed to a 100-g OGTT. [...] (Carpenter-Coustan criteria): Fasting: 95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L) 1 h: 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) 2 h: 155 mg/dL (8.6 mmol/L) 3 h: 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L)
conflicts: WHO 2013 and Uganda practice use the one-step 75-g criteria; the two-step (ACOG) pathway is US-specific and not recommended by WHO.

claim: ADA's own comparison table: glucose is inexpensive and available in most laboratories worldwide; A1C is more expensive and not as widely available globally, but needs no fasting and has low within-person variability.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Table 2.3 (Considerations related to use and interpretation of laboratory measurements of glucose and A1C)
quote: Inexpensive and available in most laboratories across the world [...] More expensive than glucose and not as widely available globally [...] Chronic measure of glucose exposure over the past ∼2–3 months

claim: Autoimmune type 1 diabetes accounts for 5-10% of diabetes and type 2 for 90-95%; DKA seldom occurs spontaneously in type 2.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Autoimmune type 1 diabetes accounts for 5–10% of diabetes [...] Type 2 diabetes accounts for 90–95% of all diabetes cases [...] DKA seldom occurs spontaneously in type 2 diabetes

claim: Early pregnancy: test those with risk factors at the first prenatal visit, screen for abnormal glucose metabolism before 15 weeks; fasting 110-125 mg/dL or A1C 5.9-6.4% marks higher risk; GDM screen at 24-28 weeks; 75-g OGTT 4-12 weeks postpartum.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Section 2 'Gestational Diabetes Mellitus' recommendations (2026 recommendation numbers not confirmed)
quote: Screen to identify abnormal glucose metabolism before 15 weeks gestation [...] Those with fasting of 110-125 or A1C of 5.9% to 6.4% are at higher risk of adverse outcomes [...] Screen those with GDM for diabetes 4-12 wks postpartum with 75-g OGTT. Lifelong screening at least every 3 yrs.
conflicts: WHO 2013: hyperglycaemia first detected at ANY time in pregnancy is classified by the same thresholds (GDM: fasting 5.1-6.9 mmol/L etc.; diabetes in pregnancy: fasting >=7.0, 2-h >=11.1, random >=11.1 with symptoms). ADA does not apply the 92 mg/dL fasting threshold before 15 weeks and instead uses 110-125 mg/dL / A1C 5.9-6.4% as an early-risk band (WHO side to be confirmed in the WHO-domain dossier).

claim: Post-transplantation diabetes mellitus (PTDM): screen after organ transplantation, make the formal diagnosis once the person is stable on immunosuppression and free of acute infection; OGTT is the preferred test.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Section 2 'Posttransplantation Diabetes Mellitus' recommendations (2026 numbers not confirmed)
quote: the 2-h PG (OGTT) testing protocol is significantly more sensitive than the other two tests and is preferentially recommended for screening for some conditions (e.g., cystic fibrosis–related diabetes or posttransplantation diabetes mellitus).

claim: ADA recommends immediate genetic testing for neonatal diabetes in anyone diagnosed in the first 6 months of life, and genetic testing for MODY in children/young adults without typical type 1 or type 2 features who often have diabetes in successive generations.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Section 2 'Monogenic Diabetes Syndromes' recommendations and Table 2.7 (2026 numbers not confirmed)

claim: Cystic-fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD) is a named specific type; OGTT (2-h PG) is the preferred screening test and A1C is not recommended for screening.
document: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Section 2 'Cystic Fibrosis-Related Diabetes' recommendations (2026 numbers not confirmed)
quote: the 2-h PG (OGTT) testing protocol is significantly more sensitive than the other two tests and is preferentially recommended for screening for some conditions (e.g., cystic fibrosis–related diabetes or posttransplantation diabetes mellitus).

claim: People with prediabetes should be monitored for progression to diabetes at least annually, adjusted to individual risk.
document: 3. Prevention or Delay of Diabetes and Associated Comorbidities: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: In people with prediabetes, monitor for the development of diabetes at least annually; modify frequency of testing based on individual risk assessment.

claim: Presymptomatic type 1 diabetes: A1C about every 6 months and a 75-g OGTT annually.
document: 3. Prevention or Delay of Diabetes and Associated Comorbidities: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: In people with presymptomatic type 1 diabetes, monitor for disease progression using A1C approximately every 6 months and 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (i.e., fasting and 2-h plasma glucose) annually;

claim: Refer adults with overweight or obesity at high risk of type 2 diabetes to a diabetes prevention programme: weight loss of at least 5-7% of initial body weight and >=150 min/week of moderate-intensity physical activity.
document: 3. Prevention or Delay of Diabetes and Associated Comorbidities: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Refer adults with overweight or obesity at high risk of type 2 diabetes to a diabetes prevention program to achieve and maintain a weight reduction of at least 5–7% of initial body weight through a healthy reduced-calorie eating pattern and ≥150 min/week of moderate-intensity physical activity.

claim: The DPP showed intensive lifestyle intervention reduces incident type 2 diabetes by 58% over 3 years; programme eligibility is overweight BMI plus laboratory risk, prior GDM or a positive risk test.
document: 3. Prevention or Delay of Diabetes and Associated Comorbidities: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
section: Narrative 'Lifestyle Behavior Change for Diabetes Prevention' / 'Delivery and Dissemination'
quote: The DPP demonstrated that intensive lifestyle intervention could reduce the risk of incident type 2 diabetes by 58% over 3 years.

claim: Prescribe an evidence-based eating pattern (e.g. Mediterranean, low carbohydrate) to people with prediabetes.
document: 3. Prevention or Delay of Diabetes and Associated Comorbidities: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Prescribe an evidence-based eating pattern (e.g., Mediterranean, low carbohydrate) to individuals with prediabetes to prevent type 2 diabetes.

claim: Metformin for type 2 diabetes prevention should be considered in high-risk adults, especially age 25-59 with BMI >=35 kg/m2, higher FPG (e.g. >=110 mg/dL), higher A1C (e.g. >=6.0%), and in those with prior GDM.
document: 3. Prevention or Delay of Diabetes and Associated Comorbidities: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Metformin for the prevention of type 2 diabetes should be considered in adults at high risk of type 2 diabetes, as typified by the Diabetes Prevention Program, especially those aged 25–59 years with BMI ≥35 kg/m2, higher fasting plasma glucose (e.g., ≥110 mg/dL [≥6 mmol/L]), and higher A1C (e.g., ≥6.0% [≥42 mmol/mol]), and in individuals with prior gestational diabetes mellitus.

claim: Consider periodic vitamin B12 measurement in people on long-term metformin, especially with anaemia or peripheral neuropathy.
document: 3. Prevention or Delay of Diabetes and Associated Comorbidities: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026

claim: ARK study (Malawi, South Africa, Uganda; iohexol-measured GFR): creatinine-based equations overestimated kidney function, made worse by ethnicity coefficients; no equation, including CKD-EPI 2021, reached P30 >= 75%; GFR < 60 was more than twice as common by measured GFR or cystatin C as by creatinine.

quote: Among 2578 included participants, creatinine-based equations overestimated kidney function compared with mGFR, worsened by use of ethnicity coefficients. document: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
section: Practice Point 1.2.3; Figure 4 (Monitoring of serum creatinine and potassium during ACEi or ARB treatment). Same text: KDIGO 2021 BP PP 3.2.5; KDIGO 2024 PP 3.6.4 and Figure 21
quote: Continue ACEi or ARB therapy unless serum creatinine rises by more than 30% within 4 weeks following initiation of treatment or an increase in dose
conflicts: Inequality differs by a hair between sources. KDIGO practice point = 'more than 30%' (so exactly 30% continues). KDIGO 2022 Figure 4, on a literal re-check, prints the two branches as '< 30% increase in creatinine' and '> 30% increase in creatinine'. KDIGO 2024 Figure 21 (unofficial mirror, p. S214) prints, on a literal re-check, '<30% decrease in eGFR' and '≥30% decrease in eGFR' - i.e. it switches the variable from creatinine rise to eGFR fall and uses ≥. ADA Rec 11.4d (A): 'Continue renin-angiotensin system blockade for mild to moderate increases in serum creatinine (≤30%) in individuals who have no signs of extracellular fluid volume depletion.' The task brief's '>= 30%' is therefore NOT the wording of the practice point; three of four statements put exactly 30% on the 'continue' side.

claim: KDIGO 2022: in T2D + CKD not at individualised glycaemic target despite metformin and SGLT2i (or unable to use them), a long-acting GLP-1 RA is recommended (1B).
document: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: In patients with T2D and CKD who have not achieved individualized glycemic targets despite use of metformin and SGLT2i treatment, or who are unable to use those medications, we recommend a long-acting GLP-1 RA (1B).
conflicts: ADA Rec 11.5b (B) is NOT conditional on glycaemia: 'To reduce cardiovascular risk and kidney disease progression in people with type 2 diabetes and CKD, a glucagon-like peptide 1 agonist with demonstrated benefit in this population is recommended.' KDIGO has signalled a change: KDIGO 2025 commentary (de Boer et al., Kidney Int 2025;107:767-771, https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/KDIGO-2025-Commentary-GLP-1-Receptor-Agonists-and-Other-Incretin-Mimetics-for-Diabetes-and-CKD.pdf): 'It is worth considering whether incretin mimetics, along with SGLT2i, should supplant metformin as a first-line treatment for T2D and CKD.' and 'KDIGO plans to address the questions discussed in this commentary in an upcoming updated clinical practice guideline.'

claim: KDIGO 2024: statin (or statin/ezetimibe) for adults >= 50 years with eGFR < 60 not on dialysis/transplant (1A); statin for adults >= 50 with CKD and eGFR >= 60 (1B); in adults 18-49 with CKD, statin if diabetes, known coronary disease, prior ischaemic stroke or 10-year coronary risk > 10% (2A); low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention only (1C).
document: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: In adults aged 18–49 years with CKD but not treated with chronic dialysis or kidney transplantation, we suggest statin treatment in people with one or more of the following (2A): known coronary disease (myocardial infarction or coronary revascularization), diabetes mellitus, prior ischemic stroke, or estimated 10-year incidence of coronary death or nonfatal myocardial infarction >10%.
conflicts: KDIGO 2022 diabetes guideline Figure 1 states simply 'A statin is recommended for all patients with T1D or T2D and CKD.' Net effect for diabetes is the same (diabetes + CKD at any adult age qualifies), but the strength differs by age band (2A at 18-49). ADA statin recommendations are in Section 10 (age 40-75 with diabetes: at least moderate-intensity statin) - out of A6 scope.

claim: KDIGO 2022: use HbA1c to monitor glycaemia in diabetes with CKD, twice a year (up to four times a year if off target or after therapy change); HbA1c accuracy and precision decline in CKD G4-G5 and are low on dialysis; a CGM-derived glucose management indicator can be used when HbA1c is discordant.
document: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: Accuracy and precision of HbA1c measurement declines with advanced CKD (G4–G5), particularly among patients treated by dialysis, in whom HbA1c measurements have low reliability.
conflicts: None. ADA Section 11 (2025): 'A1C levels are also less reliable at advanced CKD stages.'

claim: KDIGO 2022: individualised HbA1c target ranging from < 6.5% to < 8.0% in diabetes with CKD not on dialysis.
document: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: We recommend an individualized HbA1c target ranging from <6.5% to <8.0% in patients with diabetes and CKD not treated with dialysis (1C).
conflicts: ADA glycaemic goals (Section 6, outside A6 scope) default to < 7% for many non-pregnant adults with less stringent goals for limited life expectancy/hypoglycaemia risk; KDIGO gives a range and no single default. ADA-KDIGO consensus restates: 'KDIGO recommends an individualized HbA1c target of <6.5% to <8.0% for patients with diabetes and CKD'.

claim: KDIGO 2022 metformin thresholds: use when eGFR >= 30; increase eGFR monitoring when < 60; adjust (reduce) when eGFR < 45 and for some patients at 45-59; stop and do not initiate when eGFR < 30; monitor vitamin B12 after more than 4 years of treatment.
document: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: Adjust the dose of metformin when the eGFR is <45 ml/min per 1.73 m2, and for some patients when the eGFR is 45–59 ml/min per 1.73 m2 (Figure 27). [...] Monitor patients for vitamin B12 deficiency when they are treated with metformin for more than 4 years.
conflicts: ADA Section 11 (2025) agrees on the numbers: 'Metformin is contraindicated in individuals with an eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2' and 'the benefits and risks of continuing treatment should be reassessed when eGFR falls to <45 mL/min/1.73 m2.' ADA Section 3/9 advise periodic B12 testing without the '> 4 years' qualifier (outside A6 scope - check with the A-domain covering pharmacotherapy).

claim: KDIGO 2022: glycaemic management for T2D + CKD = lifestyle therapy plus first-line metformin AND an SGLT2i, with additional drugs as needed; most with eGFR >= 30 benefit from both.
document: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: Glycemic management for patients with T2D and CKD should include lifestyle therapy, first-line treatment with both metformin and a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i), and additional drug therapy as needed for glycemic control (Figure 23). [...] Most patients with T2D, CKD, and eGFR ≥30 ml/min per 1.73 m2 would benefit from treatment with both metformin and an SGLT2i.
conflicts: KDIGO 2025 commentary questions whether incretin mimetics plus SGLT2i should supplant metformin as first line (see A6-35).

claim: KDIGO 2022: maintain protein intake of 0.8 g/kg/day in diabetes with CKD not treated with dialysis (2C); 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day on dialysis.
document: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: We suggest maintaining a protein intake of 0.8 g protein/kg (weight)/d for those with diabetes and CKD not treated with dialysis (2C). [...] Patients treated with hemodialysis, and particularly peritoneal dialysis, should consume between 1.0 and 1.2 g protein/kg (weight)/d.
conflicts: Scope differs: KDIGO 2022 = all diabetes + CKD not on dialysis; KDIGO 2024 Rec 3.3.1.1 = 'adults with CKD G3-G5 (2C)'; ADA Rec 11.8 = 'non-dialysis-dependent stage G3 or higher CKD ... 0.8 g/kg body weight per day, as for the general population. A' and dialysis '1.0-1.2 g/kg/day should be considered ... B'. Same number, different evidence grades (KDIGO 2C vs ADA A).

claim: KDIGO 2022: sodium intake < 2 g/day (< 90 mmol sodium/day, or < 5 g sodium chloride/day) in diabetes with CKD (2C).
document: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
section: Recommendation 3.1.2 (2C) (identical: KDIGO 2021 BP Rec 2.1.1; KDIGO 2024 Rec 3.3.2.1)
quote: We suggest that sodium intake be <2 g of sodium per day (or <90 mmol of sodium per day, or <5 g of sodium chloride per day) in patients with diabetes and CKD (2C).
conflicts: ADA uses < 2,300 mg/day: Section 11 (2025) 'Restriction of dietary sodium (to <2,300 mg/day) may be useful to manage blood pressure and reduce cardiovascular risk'; ADA 2026 Rec 5.20 'limit sodium consumption to <2,300 mg/day'. KDIGO < 2,000 mg vs ADA < 2,300 mg. WHO population goal is also < 2 g sodium (< 5 g salt) per day.

claim: KDIGO 2022: advise moderate-intensity physical activity for a cumulative duration of at least 150 minutes per week, or to a level compatible with cardiovascular and physical tolerance (1D); avoid sedentary behaviour.
document: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: We recommend that patients with diabetes and CKD be advised to undertake moderate-intensity physical activity for a cumulative duration of at least 150 minutes per week, or to a level compatible with their cardiovascular and physical tolerance (1D).

claim: KDIGO 2022: advise people with diabetes and CKD who use tobacco to quit (1D); counsel on reducing second-hand smoke exposure.
document: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: We recommend advising patients with diabetes and CKD who use tobacco to quit using tobacco products (1D).

claim: KDIGO 2021 (carried into KDIGO 2024 Rec 3.4.1): target systolic BP < 120 mmHg, when tolerated, using STANDARDISED office BP measurement, in adults with high BP and CKD (2B).
document: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Blood Pressure in Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: We suggest that adults with high BP and CKD be treated with a target systolic blood pressure (SBP) of <120 mm Hg, when tolerated, using standardized office BP measurement (2B). [...] It is potentially hazardous to apply the recommended SBP target of <120 mm Hg to BP measurements obtained in a non-standardized manner.
conflicts: CONFLICT WITH ADA: ADA 2025 Rec 11.3 (A) 'Optimize blood pressure management (aim for <130/80 mmHg)'; ADA text 'A blood pressure level <130/80 mmHg is recommended to reduce CVD mortality and slow CKD progression among all people with diabetes.' ADA 2026 Rec 10.4 (A) narrows the gap (A6-46). KDIGO gives no diastolic target; ADA gives < 80.

claim: ADA 2026: on-treatment BP goal < 130/80 mmHg if safely attainable; a systolic goal < 120 mmHg should be encouraged in people with high cardiovascular or kidney risk.

quote: If it can be safely attained, the on-treatment blood pressure goal is <130/80 mmHg; a systolic blood pressure goal <120 mmHg should be encouraged in individuals with high cardiovascular or kidney risk.
conflicts: ADA 2025 Section 11 Rec 11.3 said only 'aim for <130/80 mmHg' for CKD; ADA 2026 moves toward KDIGO's SBP < 120 for those with kidney risk (text cites the BPROAD trial). KDIGO: SBP < 120 for all adults with high BP and CKD when tolerated, standardised measurement, no diastolic target (A6-45).

claim: KDIGO 2024 Figure 48: circumstances for referral of adults to specialist kidney care.
document: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: eGFR <30 ml/min per 1.73 m2 [...] A sustained fall in GFR of >20% or >30% in those people initiating hemodynamically active therapies [...] A consistent finding of ACR >700 mg/g [>70 mg/mmol] [...] Urinary red cell casts, RBC >20 per high power field sustained and not readily explained [...] CKD and hypertension refractory to treatment ≥4 antihypertensive agents
conflicts: CHANGED FROM KDIGO 2012 Rec 5.1.1 (A6-48): in 2012 A3 albuminuria alone (ACR >= 300 mg/g) triggered referral; in 2024 it is A3 WITH haematuria, or ACR > 700 mg/g, or doubling. 2012's 'progression of CKD' (25% drop with category change; > 5 mL/min/1.73 m2/yr) is replaced by 'sustained fall in GFR of >20%' and a kidney-failure-risk criterion. ADA: refer if eGFR < 30, continuously rising UACR / falling eGFR, uncertain aetiology, difficult management issues (A6-51). ADA-KDIGO heat map marks every A3 cell and G3b A2 as 'Treat and refer' (A6-07) - i.e. the diabetes consensus still refers on A3 alone.

claim: KDIGO 2012 Rec 5.1.1 (1B): refer for AKI or abrupt sustained fall in GFR; GFR < 30; consistent ACR >= 300 mg/g; progression of CKD; red cell casts or RBC > 20/hpf; hypertension refractory to >= 4 agents; persistent potassium abnormalities; recurrent or extensive nephrolithiasis; hereditary kidney disease.
document: KDIGO 2012 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: a consistent finding of significant albuminuria (ACR ≥300 mg/g [≥30 mg/mmol] or AER ≥300 mg/24 hours, approximately equivalent to PCR ≥500 mg/g [≥50 mg/mmol] or PER ≥500 mg/24 hours) [...] urinary red cell casts, RBC >20 per high power field sustained and not readily explained [...] CKD and hypertension refractory to treatment with 4 or more antihypertensive agents
conflicts: Superseded by KDIGO 2024 Figure 48 (A6-47), which narrows the albuminuria criterion and replaces the progression definition. Kept because the task brief and many national adaptations still quote the 2012 list.

claim: Definitions of progression: KDIGO 2012 - drop in GFR category with >= 25% fall in eGFR from baseline; RAPID progression = sustained decline in eGFR of MORE THAN 5 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year. KDIGO 2024 - a change in eGFR > 20% (or > 30% after starting haemodynamically active therapy) or a doubling of ACR exceeds expected variability and warrants evaluation.
document: KDIGO 2012 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease ; KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
section: KDIGO 2012 statement 2.1.3 (Not Graded); KDIGO 2024 Practice Points 2.1.3, 2.1.4, 2.1.5
quote: A certain drop in eGFR is defined as a drop in GFR category accompanied by a 25% or greater drop in eGFR from baseline. Rapid progression is defined as a sustained decline in eGFR of more than 5 ml/min/1.73 m2/yr.
conflicts: The task brief wrote '>= 5 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year'; the source says 'MORE THAN 5' (strict >). KDIGO 2024 no longer prints the 5 mL/min/yr or 25% definitions; ADA Rec 11.10 says 'rapidly progressing kidney disease' without a number. So the only numeric definition of 'rapid' is KDIGO 2012's, now superseded by the 2024 '> 20%' trigger.

claim: KDIGO 2024: in CKD G3-G5 use a validated kidney-failure risk equation; 5-year risk of 3%-5% can prompt nephrology referral; 2-year risk > 10% multidisciplinary care; 2-year risk > 40% KRT preparation.
document: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: A 5-year kidney failure risk of 3%–5% can be used to determine need for nephrology referral in addition to criteria based on eGFR or urine ACR, and other clinical considerations.

claim: ADA: refer to a nephrologist for continuously rising urinary albumin and/or continuously falling eGFR and/or eGFR < 30 (A); and for uncertain aetiology, difficult management issues and rapidly progressing kidney disease (B).
version: 2025 (Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl 1):S239-S251) - 2026 edition (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S246, doi 10.2337/dc26-S011) could NOT be opened (diabetesjournals.org 403; PMC id not found / PMC CAPTCHA)

A [...] Refer to a nephrologist for uncertainty about the etiology of kidney disease, difficult management issues, and rapidly progressing kidney disease. B
conflicts: ADA gives no numeric definition of 'continuously' or 'rapidly'; KDIGO 2024 gives > 20% sustained fall and ACR doubling (A6-47, A6-49). ADA does not list haematuria/red-cell casts as a separate referral bullet but treats active urinary sediment as pointing to non-diabetic disease (A6-52).

claim: ADA: active urinary sediment, rapidly increasing albuminuria or total proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, rapidly decreasing eGFR, or absence of retinopathy (in type 1 diabetes) suggest an alternative or additional cause of kidney disease.
version: 2025 (Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl 1):S239-S251) - 2026 edition (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S246, doi 10.2337/dc26-S011) could NOT be opened (diabetesjournals.org 403; PMC id not found / PMC CAPTCHA)
document: 11. Chronic Kidney Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2025

quote: An active urinary sediment (containing red or white blood cells or cellular casts), rapidly increasing albuminuria or total proteinuria, the presence of nephrotic syndrome, rapidly decreasing eGFR, or the absence of retinopathy (in type 1 diabetes) suggests alternative or additional causes of kidney disease.
conflicts: The task brief's 'short diabetes duration in type 1 < 5 years' is NOT stated as a red flag in this sentence; it is an inference from 'CKD in people with diabetes typically develops after a duration of 10 years in type 1 diabetes (the most common presentation is 5-15 years after the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes) but may be present at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes.' and from the screening start at >= 5 years. KDIGO 2022 has no equivalent list.

claim: ADA (2025 text): in T2D + CKD, SGLT2 inhibitor with demonstrated benefit if eGFR >= 20 (A); GLP-1 RA with demonstrated benefit to reduce CV risk and kidney disease progression (B); in CKD with albuminuria, non-steroidal MRA if eGFR >= 25 with potassium monitoring (A).
version: 2025 (Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl 1):S239-S251) - 2026 edition (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S246, doi 10.2337/dc26-S011) could NOT be opened (diabetesjournals.org 403; PMC id not found / PMC CAPTCHA)
document: 11. Chronic Kidney Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2025
quote: For people with type 2 diabetes and CKD, use of a sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor with demonstrated benefit is recommended to reduce CKD progression and cardiovascular events in individuals with eGFR ≥20 mL/min/1.73 m2. A
conflicts: KDIGO 2022 positions GLP-1 RA only when glycaemic targets are not met on metformin + SGLT2i (A6-35). ADA 11.5c does not print an albuminuria number or 'T2D' in the recommendation sentence as extracted ('in people with CKD and albuminuria'); KDIGO specifies T2D, albuminuria >= 30 mg/g, normal potassium and maximal RASi (A6-33).

claim: ADA: aim to reduce urinary albumin by >= 30% in people with CKD and albuminuria >= 300 mg/g to slow CKD progression (B).
version: 2025 (Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl 1):S239-S251) - 2026 edition (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S246, doi 10.2337/dc26-S011) could NOT be opened (diabetesjournals.org 403; PMC id not found / PMC CAPTCHA)

quote: Aim to reduce urinary albumin by ≥30% in people with CKD and albuminuria ≥300 mg/g to slow CKD progression.
conflicts: KDIGO sets no albuminuria-reduction target; KDIGO 2024 PP 2.1.5 treats a doubling of ACR as a signal to evaluate.

claim: KDIGO AKI definition: rise in serum creatinine by >= 0.3 mg/dL (>= 26.5 umol/L) within 48 hours; or to >= 1.5 times baseline known or presumed to have occurred within the prior 7 days; or urine volume < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours.
document: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury
quote: AKI is defined as any of the following (Not Graded): Increase in SCr by ≥0.3 mg/dl (≥26.5 μmol/l) within 48 hours; or Increase in SCr to ≥1.5 times baseline, which is known or presumed to have occurred within the prior 7 days; or Urine volume <0.5 ml/kg/h for 6 hours.
conflicts: ADA Section 11 gives no numbers: 'Acute kidney injury (AKI) is diagnosed by a sustained increase in serum creatinine over a short period of time.' and warns that creatinine rises up to 30% on RAS blockers 'must not be confused with AKI'. A 30% rise is below the 1.5x criterion but can exceed 26.5 umol/L in absolute terms when baseline creatinine is above ~88 umol/L - the engine must suppress the AKI flag for an expected post-RASi/SGLT2i change only by rule the CSO approves.

claim: KDIGO AKI staging by serum creatinine and urine output (stages 1-3).
document: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury
quote: Stage 1: 1.5–1.9 times baseline OR ≥0.3 mg/dl (≥26.5 μmol/l) increase; <0.5 ml/kg/h for 6–12 hours. Stage 2: 2.0–2.9 times baseline; <0.5 ml/kg/h for ≥12 hours. Stage 3: 3.0 times baseline OR increase in serum creatinine to ≥4.0 mg/dl (≥353.6 μmol/l) OR initiation of renal replacement therapy; <0.3 ml/kg/h for ≥24 hours OR anuria for ≥12 hours

claim: KDIGO 2024 names the SADMANS sick-day list (sulfonylureas, ACEi, diuretics/direct renin inhibitors, metformin, ARBs, NSAIDs, SGLT2i) but states there is a paucity of evidence that sick-day rules prevent AKI and that data suggest potential harm from errors.
document: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
section: Section 4.3 text and Figure 47 (Essential steps for appropriate sick day rule implementation), page S251; Practice Point 4.3.2
quote: Patients receive guidance to temporarily stop the following medications: sulfonylureas, ACEi, diuretics/direct renin inhibitors, metformin, ARBs, NSAIDs, and SGLT2i (often described with the acronym SADMANS). [...] There is a paucity of evidence to support sick day rules to prevent AKI or other clinically relevant outcomes.
conflicts: KDIGO describes SADMANS but does NOT endorse blanket patient-initiated sick-day rules: 'Instead, data suggest potential harm if people make mistakes in recognizing dehydrating illness or about which drugs to stop and when to restart.' Diabetes Canada and some UK bodies do recommend SADMANS (not opened; outside the listed sources). ADA Section 11 has no SADMANS list in the text read.

claim: KDIGO 2024: consider planned discontinuation of metformin, ACEi, ARBs and SGLT2i in the 48-72 hours before elective surgery or during acute management of adverse effects; withhold SGLT2i during prolonged fasting, surgery or critical illness.
document: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease

claim: KDIGO 2024 Figure 32: actions to manage hyperkalaemia are triggered at potassium > 5.5 mmol/L - first correct other factors, then diuretics/bicarbonate/potassium exchange agents, and reduce or stop RASi/MRA only as a last resort.
document: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
quote: Figure 32 | Actions to manage hyperkalemia (potassium>5.5 mmol/l) in chronic kidney disease. [...] Review non-RASi medications (e.g. NSAIDs, trimethoprim) [...] Appropriate use of diuretics [...] Optimize serum bicarbonate levels [...] Licensed potassium exchange agents [...] Reduce dose or discontinue RASi/MRA
conflicts: The KDIGO RASi monitoring algorithms (KDIGO 2022 Figure 4; KDIGO 2024 Figure 21) print NO potassium number - they branch on 'normokalemia' vs 'hyperkalemia' (A6-61). The only numeric gates are Figure 32 (> 5.5), Table 28 (6.0-6.4; >= 6.5) and the finerenone figure (<= 4.8 / 4.9-5.5 / > 5.5 / <= 5.0). ADA gives no potassium number in Section 11 recommendations.

claim: KDIGO 2024 Table 28: moderate hyperkalaemia K+ 6.0-6.4 mmol/L (assess and treat in hospital if clinically unwell or AKI; repeat within 24 hours if an unexpected result); severe K+ >= 6.5 mmol/L (immediate assessment and treatment including blood tests and ECG monitoring).
document: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
section: Table 28 (Suggested action in the event of moderate and severe hyperkalemia), page S227
quote: Moderate K+ 6.0–6.4 mmol/l: Clinically unwell or AKI - Assess and treat in hospital; Unexpected result - Repeat within 24 hours. Severe K+ ≥6.5 mmol/l: Take immediate action to assess and treat. Assessment will include blood testing and electrocardiogram monitoring
conflicts: Table 28 has no 'mild' band (no 5.5-5.9 row on the page). Other bodies band differently (e.g. UK Kidney Association: mild 5.5-5.9, moderate 6.0-6.4, severe >= 6.5 - from memory, not opened). Emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia is outside A6 and no doses are recorded.

claim: The KDIGO ACEi/ARB monitoring algorithm branches on normokalaemia vs hyperkalaemia without a numeric potassium threshold; for hyperkalaemia it lists: review concurrent drugs, moderate potassium intake, consider diuretics, sodium bicarbonate, potassium binders; reduce or stop only if mitigation is ineffective.
document: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
section: Figure 21 (Algorithm for monitoring of potassium and eGFR after the initiation of RASi), page S214; same content in KDIGO 2022 Figure 4
quote: Monitor serum creatinine and potassium (within 2–4 weeks after starting or changing dose) [...] Review concurrent drugs [...] Moderate dietary potassium intake [...] Consider: diuretics, sodium bicarbonate, potassium binders [...] Reduce dose or stop ACEi or ARB if mitigation strategies ineffective
conflicts: The task brief expected 'potassium > 5.5 mmol/L in the RASi algorithm': the number is NOT in the RASi algorithm; it is in the separate hyperkalaemia figure (A6-59). CSO should decide the numeric gate the engine uses for RASi (e.g. > 5.5 mmol/L per Figure 32).

quote: Repeat this application twice, but alternate this with at least one 'mock' application in which the tuning fork is not vibrating. The test is positive if the patient correctly answers at least two out of three applications, and negative if two out of three answers are incorrect.

claim: IWGDF light touch (Ipswich Touch) test: used when no monofilament or tuning fork is available; examiner lightly touches the tips of the 1st, 3rd and 5th toes of both feet for 1-2 s; LOPS is likely when touch is not sensed at 2 or more sites.
document: Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease (IWGDF 2023 update)
quote: This simple test (also called the Ipswich Touch test) can be used to screen for loss of protective sensation (LOPS), when the 10 gram monofilament or 128 HZ tuning fork is not available. [...] lightly sequentially touches with the tip of hers/his index finger the tips of the first, third, and fifth toes of both feet for 1–2 s [...] LOPS is likely when light touch is not sensed in ≥ 2 sites

claim: ADA: the 10-g monofilament should be combined with at least one other neurological test; absent monofilament sensation plus one other abnormal test confirms LOPS.
document: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S261–S276; doi 10.2337/dc26-S012)
quote: One of the most useful tests to determine LOPS is the 10-g monofilament test. The monofilament test should be performed with at least one other neurologic assessment tool (e.g., pinprick, temperature perception, ankle reflexes, or vibratory perception with a 128-Hz tuning fork or similar device). Absent monofilament sensation and one other abnormal test confirm the presence of LOPS.
conflicts: IWGDF 2023: LOPS can be established by one technique alone (monofilament OR tuning fork, or Ipswich touch test). Earlier ADA editions said 'Absent monofilament sensation suggests LOPS, while at least two normal tests (and no abnormal test) rules out LOPS' - the 2026 text was checked and does NOT contain the 'two normal tests rule out LOPS' sentence.

claim: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS: in a person with diabetes without a foot ulcer, take a PAD history, examine for ischaemia and palpate foot pulses at least annually or with any change in the feet; the same clinical examination is required in anyone with a foot ulcer or gangrene.
document: The intersocietal IWGDF, ESVS, SVS guidelines on peripheral artery disease in patients with diabetes mellitus and a foot ulcer (2023)
quote: In a person with diabetes without a foot ulcer, take a relevant history for peripheral artery disease, examine the foot for signs of ischaemia and palpate the foot pulses at least annually, or with any change in clinical status of the feet.

claim: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS: PAD is less likely with ABI 0.9-1.3, TBI >= 0.70 and triphasic or biphasic pedal Doppler waveforms; no single test is optimal and no value excludes PAD; in a person with an ulcer or gangrene all three should be evaluated.
document: The intersocietal IWGDF, ESVS, SVS guidelines on peripheral artery disease in patients with diabetes mellitus and a foot ulcer (2023)
quote: No single modality has been shown to be optimal for diagnosis of PAD, and there is no value above which PAD can be excluded. However, PAD is less likely in the presence of ABI 0.9-1.3; TBI ≥ 0.70; and triphasic or biphasic pedal Doppler waveforms.
conflicts: TBI threshold is 0.70 in the 2023 guideline (the 2019 IWGDF guideline used >= 0.75). The IWGDF 2023 practical guidelines repeat 0.70. ADA 2026 gives no ABI/TBI cut-offs in Section 12.

claim: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS: medial artery calcification falsely elevates ankle (and to a lesser extent toe) pressures; an elevated ABI (>1.3) is itself a risk marker for amputation.
document: The intersocietal IWGDF, ESVS, SVS guidelines on peripheral artery disease in patients with diabetes mellitus and a foot ulcer (2023)
quote: Other research has demonstrated an elevated ABI (>1.3) is associated with both greater likelihood of amputation and worse amputation free survival outcomes and therefore should be recognised as a risk factor for poor DFU outcomes.

claim: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS rationale: a TBI <0.70 and a visual monophasic pedal Doppler waveform each have only moderate ability to diagnose and exclude PAD.
document: The intersocietal IWGDF, ESVS, SVS guidelines on peripheral artery disease in patients with diabetes mellitus and a foot ulcer (2023)
quote: A TBI <0.70 has a moderate ability to diagnose and exclude PAD

claim: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS: ankle pressure and ABI are weak predictors of healing; ankle pressure <50 mmHg or ABI <0.5 may be associated with impaired healing and major amputation.
document: The intersocietal IWGDF, ESVS, SVS guidelines on peripheral artery disease in patients with diabetes mellitus and a foot ulcer (2023)
quote: Ankle pressure and ABI are weak predictors of healing. A low ankle pressure (e.g. < 50 mmHg) or ABI (e.g. < 0.5) may be associated with greater likelihood of impaired healing and greater likelihood of major amputation.
conflicts: Rec 6 uses ABI <0.5 as the prognostic example, whereas Rec 13 (urgent vascular consult) and the practical guidelines use ABI <0.4.

claim: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS: toe pressure >= 30 mmHg raises the pre-test probability of healing by up to 30%; <30 mmHg raises the probability of major amputation by about 20%.
document: The intersocietal IWGDF, ESVS, SVS guidelines on peripheral artery disease in patients with diabetes mellitus and a foot ulcer (2023)
quote: consider performing a toe pressure measurement in order to assess likelihood of healing and amputation. A toe pressure ≥ 30 mmHg increases the pre-test probability of healing by up to 30% and a value <30mmHg increases the pretest probability of major amputation by approximately 20%.
conflicts: ADA 2026 (narrative): 'Toe systolic blood pressure <30 mmHg is suggestive of PAD and an inability to heal foot ulcerations' - same threshold, more categorical wording.

claim: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS: if toe pressure cannot be done, TcPO2 >= 25 mmHg raises the probability of healing by up to 45% (<25 mmHg raises major amputation probability by about 20%); skin perfusion pressure >= 40 mmHg raises healing probability by up to 30%.
document: The intersocietal IWGDF, ESVS, SVS guidelines on peripheral artery disease in patients with diabetes mellitus and a foot ulcer (2023)
quote: A TcPO2 ≥ 25 mmHg increases the pre-test probability of healing by up to 45% and value < 25 mmHg has been shown to increase the pre-test probability of major amputation by approximately 20%. An SPP ≥ 40mmHg increases the pre-test probability of healing by up to 30%.

claim: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS Rec 13: severe ischaemia = ABI <0.4, ankle pressure <50 mmHg, toe pressure <30 mmHg, TcPO2 <30 mmHg, or monophasic/absent pedal Doppler waveforms - urgently consult a vascular specialist about revascularisation.
document: The intersocietal IWGDF, ESVS, SVS guidelines on peripheral artery disease in patients with diabetes mellitus and a foot ulcer (2023)
quote: In a person with diabetes, peripheral artery disease, a foot ulcer, and severe ischaemia i.e. an ankle-brachial index <0.4, ankle pressure <50mmHg, toe pressure <30mmHg or transcutaneous oxygen pressure <30mmHg or monophasic or absent pedal Doppler waveforms, urgently consult a vascular specialist regarding possible revascularisation.
conflicts: INTERNAL IWGDF DISCREPANCY: Rec 13 of the PAD guideline gives TcPO2 <30 mmHg, whereas the IWGDF 2023 practical guidelines (section 4.2.2) give 'TcpO2 is <25 mmHg' for the same urgent-assessment trigger, and PAD Rec 8 uses 25 mmHg for prognosis. Re-checked on a second fetch: Rec 13 reads 30.

claim: IWGDF practical guidelines: ankle pressure <50 mmHg or ABI <0.4 - consider urgent vascular imaging and revascularisation; also consider urgent assessment if toe pressure <30 mmHg or TcPO2 <25 mmHg.
document: Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease (IWGDF 2023 update)
quote: In a person with either an ankle pressure <50mm Hg or an ABI <0.4 consider urgent vascular imaging, always with detailed visualization of below-the knee and pedal arteries, and revascularisation. Also consider urgent assessment for revascularisation if the toe pressure is <30mmHg or TcpO2 is <25 mmHg.
conflicts: TcPO2 25 mmHg here vs 30 mmHg in PAD guideline Rec 13 (see previous item).

claim: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS Rec 15: if the wound deteriorates or fails to improve significantly (e.g. <50% area reduction within 4 weeks) despite appropriate care, reassess vascular status and consult a vascular specialist.
document: The intersocietal IWGDF, ESVS, SVS guidelines on peripheral artery disease in patients with diabetes mellitus and a foot ulcer (2023)
quote: when the wound deteriorates or fails to significantly improve (e.g. a less than 50% reduction in wound area within 4 weeks) despite appropriate infection and glucose control, wound care, and offloading, reassess the vascular status and consult with a vascular specialist
conflicts: IWGDF practical guidelines 2023 section 4.2.2: 'When an ulcer fails to show signs of healing within 4-6 weeks, despite optimal management, consider angiography and revascularisation.' (4-6 weeks vs 4 weeks with a 50% area criterion).

claim: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS Rec 9: always assess for PAD and other causes of poor healing; diabetic microangiopathy must not be assumed to be the primary cause of ulceration, gangrene or poor healing.
document: The intersocietal IWGDF, ESVS, SVS guidelines on peripheral artery disease in patients with diabetes mellitus and a foot ulcer (2023)
quote: Diabetes-related microangiopathy should not be considered the primary cause of foot ulceration, gangrene or poor wound healing without excluding other causes.

claim: ADA: initial PAD screening = lower-extremity pulses, capillary refill time, rubor on dependency, pallor on elevation and venous filling time; refer for ABI with toe pressures those with leg fatigue, claudication, rest pain relieved by dependency, or decreased/absent pedal pulses.
document: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S261–S276; doi 10.2337/dc26-S012)
quote: Initial screening for peripheral artery disease (PAD) should include assessment of lower-extremity pulses, capillary refill time, rubor on dependency, pallor on elevation, and venous filling time. Individuals with a history of leg fatigue, claudication, and rest pain relieved with dependency or decreased or absent pedal pulses should be referred for ankle-brachial index with toe pressures

claim: ADA Section 10 (cardiovascular disease) is believed to recommend ABI screening for asymptomatic PAD in older people with diabetes or those with microvascular disease/foot complications/long duration - NOT VERIFIED.
document: 10. Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes
section: Recommendation on screening for asymptomatic PAD (number not confirmed)

claim: IWGDF/IDSA: grade 1 = uninfected (no systemic or local signs); infection = at least two of local swelling/induration, erythema >0.5 cm, tenderness/pain, warmth, purulent discharge, with no other cause of skin inflammation; grade 2 (mild) = skin/subcutaneous tissue only with erythema <2 cm around the wound and no systemic signs.
document: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of foot infection in persons with diabetes (IWGDF/IDSA 2023)
section: Table 1: classification system for defining the presence and severity of foot infection
quote: Infected: At least two of these items are present: Local swelling or induration; Erythema > 0.5 but < 2 cm around the wound; Local tenderness or pain; Local increased warmth; Purulent discharge. And, no other cause of an inflammatory response of the skin (e.g., trauma, gout, acute Charcot neuro-arthropathy, fracture, thrombosis, or venous stasis)

claim: IWGDF/IDSA grade 3 (moderate): infection without systemic manifestations but with erythema extending >= 2 cm from the wound margin and/or involving tissue deeper than skin and subcutaneous tissue.
document: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of foot infection in persons with diabetes (IWGDF/IDSA 2023)
quote: Infection with no systemic manifestations and involving: erythema extending ≥ 2 cm from the wound margin, and/or tissue deeper than skin and subcutaneous tissues (e.g., tendon, muscle, joint, and bone)

claim: IWGDF/IDSA grade 4 (severe): any foot infection with >= 2 SIRS criteria - temperature >38 C or <36 C; heart rate >90/min; respiratory rate >20/min or PaCO2 <4.3 kPa (32 mmHg); white cell count >12,000/mm3 or <4 G/L or >10% band forms.
document: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of foot infection in persons with diabetes (IWGDF/IDSA 2023)
quote: Any foot infection with associated systemic manifestations (of the systemic inflammatory response syndrome [SIRS]) as manifested by ≥ 2 of the following: temperature, > 38°C or < 36°C; heart rate, > 90 beats/min; respiratory rate, >20 breaths/min, or PaCO2 < 4.3 kPa (32 mmHg); white blood cell count >12,000/mm3, or < 4G/L, or > 10% immature (band) forms

claim: IWGDF/IDSA: add '(O)' to grade 3 or 4 when infection involves bone (osteomyelitis) - i.e. 3(O) or 4(O).
document: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of foot infection in persons with diabetes (IWGDF/IDSA 2023)
quote: Infection involving bone (osteomyelitis)

claim: IWGDF/IDSA Rec 2: consider hospitalising everyone with a severe (grade 4) foot infection, and those with a moderate (grade 3) infection associated with key relevant morbidities.
document: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of foot infection in persons with diabetes (IWGDF/IDSA 2023)
quote: Consider hospitalising all persons with diabetes and a foot infection who have either a severe foot infection as classified by the IWGDF/IDSA classification, or a moderate infection which is associated with key relevant morbidities.

claim: IWGDF/IDSA Rec 18: obtain urgent surgical consultation for severe infection, or moderate infection complicated by extensive gangrene, necrotising infection, deep (below-fascia) abscess, compartment syndrome or severe lower-limb ischaemia.
document: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of foot infection in persons with diabetes (IWGDF/IDSA 2023)
quote: Urgent surgical consultation should be obtained in cases of severe infection or moderate diabetes-related foot infection complicated by extensive gangrene, necrotizing infection, signs suggesting deep (below the fascia) abscess, compartment syndrome, or severe lower limb ischaemia.

claim: IWGDF: diagnose soft-tissue infection clinically - at least two signs or symptoms of inflammation (redness, warmth, induration, pain/tenderness) or purulent secretions - and grade severity with the IWGDF/IDSA scheme.
document: Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease (IWGDF 2023 update)
quote: Diagnose infection by the presence of at least two clinical signs or symptoms of inflammation (redness, warmth, induration, pain/tenderness) or purulent secretions.

claim: IWGDF: osteomyelitis is likely with a positive probe-to-bone test plus plain X-ray abnormalities; initial work-up = probe-to-bone + plain X-ray + ESR or CRP or procalcitonin; MRI when still in doubt.
document: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of foot infection in persons with diabetes (IWGDF/IDSA 2023)
quote: consider using a combination of probe-to-bone test, plain X-rays, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, or C-reactive protein, or procalcitonin as the initial studies

claim: SINBAD scores six items 0 or 1 - Site (forefoot 0; midfoot/hindfoot 1), Ischaemia (at least one palpable pulse 0; reduced pedal flow 1), Neuropathy (protective sensation intact 0; lost 1), Bacterial infection (none 0; present 1), Area (<1 cm2 0; >=1 cm2 1), Depth (skin/subcutaneous 0; muscle, tendon or deeper 1) - maximum 6.
document: Guidelines on the classification of foot ulcers in people with diabetes (IWGDF 2023 update)
quote: creating an easy-to-use scoring system that can achieve a maximum of 6 points

claim: IWGDF: use SINBAD for communication between professionals (stating each variable) and for regional/national/international audit; consider WIfI where expertise and resources exist, and in PAD to stratify healing likelihood and amputation risk; use IWGDF/IDSA to classify infection; do not use any system for individual prognosis.
document: Guidelines on the classification of foot ulcers in people with diabetes (IWGDF 2023 update)
quote: In a person with diabetes and a foot ulcer, use the SINBAD system for communication about the characteristics of an ulcer between healthcare professionals, and clearly stating the presence or absence of each of the composing variables. (Strength of recommendation: Strong; Certainty of evidence: Low)

claim: IWGDF: describe ulcer type as neuropathic (LOPS, no PAD), neuro-ischaemic (LOPS and PAD) or ischaemic (PAD, no LOPS).
document: Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease (IWGDF 2023 update)
quote: In addition, the ulcer type can be described as neuropathic (LOPS, but no PAD), neuro-ischaemic (LOPS and PAD), or ischaemic (PAD, but no LOPS).

claim: IWGDF: always consider active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy in a person with diabetes, neuropathy and intact skin who has increased temperature, oedema and/or redness of one foot compared with the other.
document: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy in persons with diabetes mellitus (IWGDF 2023)
quote: Always consider active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy in a person with diabetes mellitus, neuropathy and intact skin when there are clinical findings of an increase in temperature, oedema, and/or redness of the foot, compared to the contralateral foot.

claim: IWGDF does NOT endorse a numeric skin-temperature threshold for diagnosing active Charcot: 2 C (or 4 F = 2.2 C) has been used in publications, but no diagnostic-accuracy evidence was found; it suggests infrared thermometry and calculating the left-right difference at the same anatomical point.
document: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy in persons with diabetes mellitus (IWGDF 2023)
quote: An increase in skin temperature of 2° Celsius or 4° Fahrenheit (which is actually 2.2° Celsius) of the involved foot compared to the same location on the uninvolved foot has been used as a diagnostic threshold for active CNO in several publications.
conflicts: NICE NG19 1.7.7 does use a number, but for resolution not diagnosis: 'Acute Charcot arthropathy is likely to resolve when there is a sustained temperature difference of less than 2 degrees between both feet.' IWGDF practical guidelines: 'Unfortunately, there is currently no absolute cut-off value to define remission of CNO.' ADA 2026 mentions no temperature difference.

claim: IWGDF: start knee-high immobilisation/offloading promptly as soon as active Charcot is suspected, while investigations proceed.
document: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy in persons with diabetes mellitus (IWGDF 2023)
quote: Initiate knee high immobilization/offloading promptly while further diagnostic studies are performed to confirm or rule out active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy (CNO) when active CNO is suspected in a person with diabetes mellitus and intact skin.
conflicts: NICE NG19 1.7.3: 'Offer non-weight-bearing treatment until definitive treatment can be started by the multidisciplinary foot care service.' ADA 2026: 'These individuals require total non–weight-bearing and urgent referral to a foot care specialist'. IWGDF specifies the device (knee-high), NICE/ADA specify non-weight-bearing.

claim: IWGDF device hierarchy for active Charcot with intact skin: 1st non-removable knee-high total contact cast; 2nd knee-high walker rendered non-removable; 3rd removable knee-high device worn at all times; below-ankle devices not recommended.
document: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy in persons with diabetes mellitus (IWGDF 2023)
quote: Use a non-removable knee-high device to immobilise and offload the foot to promote remission of the disease, and prevention or progression of deformity in a person with active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy and intact skin.
