claim: IWGDF: plain X-ray of foot and ankle (ideally bilateral, weight-bearing; AP, medial oblique and lateral foot views; AP, mortise and lateral ankle views); MRI if X-ray is normal; if MRI unavailable, scintigraphy, CT or SPECT-CT; do not use CRP, ESR, white cell count or alkaline phosphatase to diagnose or exclude.
document: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy in persons with diabetes mellitus (IWGDF 2023)
quote: Perform Magnetic Resonance Imaging in a person with diabetes mellitus and suspected active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy with normal appearance of the plain X-rays to diagnose or exclude the disease and its activity.

claim: IWGDF: remission is judged on temperature, oedema and imaging together; there is no absolute temperature cut-off; the cast can stop when there are no clinical signs of inflammation and fractures have consolidated on X-ray.
document: Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy in persons with diabetes mellitus (IWGDF 2023)
quote: We suggest that the findings of temperature measurement, clinical oedema, and imaging should all be considered when concluding that active Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy is in remission.

claim: ADA: a warm, swollen, red foot without an open ulcer in a person with neuropathy needs work-up for Charcot neuroarthropathy, foot and ankle X-rays, total non-weight-bearing and urgent referral to a foot care specialist.
document: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S261–S276; doi 10.2337/dc26-S012)
quote: Special consideration should be given to individuals with neuropathy who present with a warm, swollen, red foot with or without a history of trauma and without an open ulceration. These individuals require a thorough workup for possible Charcot neuroarthropathy (140,141). Foot and ankle X-rays should be performed in all individuals presenting with the above clinical findings.

claim: IWGDF's five key elements of foot ulcer prevention: identify the at-risk foot; regularly inspect and examine; structured education; routine appropriate footwear; treat risk factors for ulceration.
document: Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease (IWGDF 2023 update)
quote: 1. Identify the person with an at-risk foot 2. Regularly inspect and examine the feet of a person at-risk for foot ulceration 3. Provide structured education for patients, their family and healthcare professionals 4. Encourage routine wearing of appropriate footwear 5. Treat risk factors for ulceration

claim: IWGDF education items for the at-risk person include: daily inspection of both feet including between the toes; never barefoot, in socks only or in thin-soled slippers; check inside shoes; wash daily in water below 37 C and dry between toes; no heaters/hot-water bottles; no chemical corn removers; emollients but not between toes; cut nails straight across; regular professional foot examination.
document: Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease (IWGDF 2023 update)
quote: Avoid walking barefoot, in socks without footwear, or in thin-soled slippers, whether at home or outside [...] Wash feet daily (with water temperature always below 37°C), and dry them carefully, especially between the toes [...] Do not use any kind of heater or a hot-water bottle to warm feet [...] Cut toenails straight across

claim: IWGDF: the inside length of the shoe should be 1-2 cm longer than the foot; inappropriate footwear and barefoot walking are major causes of the trauma that leads to ulceration.
document: Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease (IWGDF 2023 update)
section: Section 3.4 Routine wearing of appropriate footwear
quote: In persons with diabetes and IWGDF risk category 1 or higher, wearing inappropriate footwear or walking barefoot are major causes of foot trauma leading to foot ulceration.

claim: IWGDF: treat excess callus, ingrown toenails and fungal infections, and treat any modifiable pre-ulcerative sign on the foot.
document: Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease (IWGDF 2023 update)
section: Section 3.5 Treating risk factors for ulceration
quote: Provide appropriate treatment of excess callus on the foot, for ingrown toe nails, and for fungal infections on the foot. Treat any (modifiable) pre-ulcerative sign on the foot

claim: IWGDF 2023 organises ulcer treatment under: 4.2.1 treatment of foot infection; 4.2.2 restoration of tissue perfusion; 4.2.3A pressure offloading and ulcer protection; 4.2.3B local ulcer care; 4.2.4 person-centred care (glycaemia, oedema, malnutrition, cardiovascular risk, depression/psychosocial).
document: Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease (IWGDF 2023 update)
quote: Foot ulcers will heal in the majority of patients if the clinician bases treatment on the principles outlined below.
conflicts: The 2019 IWGDF practical guidelines used a different six-item list and order (pressure offloading and ulcer protection; restoration of tissue perfusion; treatment of infection; metabolic control and treatment of co-morbidities; local ulcer care; education for patient and relatives) - that older list is the one in the task brief. In 2023 metabolic control and education are folded into 'Person-centred care'.

claim: IWGDF: the preferred offloading for a neuropathic plantar ulcer is a non-removable knee-high device - total contact cast or a removable walker rendered irremovable.
document: Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease (IWGDF 2023 update)
section: Section 4.2.3A Pressure offloading and ulcer protection
quote: The preferred offloading treatment for a neuropathic plantar ulcer is a non-removable knee-high offloading device, i.e, either a total contact cast (TCC) or removable walker rendered (by the provider fitting it) irremovable.

claim: NICE NG19: refer IMMEDIATELY to acute services (and inform the multidisciplinary foot care service) for ulceration with fever or any signs of sepsis, ulceration with limb ischaemia, suspected deep-seated soft tissue or bone infection, or gangrene.
document: Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management (NICE guideline NG19)
quote: Examples of limb-threatening and life-threatening diabetic foot problems include the following: Ulceration with fever or any signs of sepsis. Ulceration with limb ischaemia (see the NICE guideline on peripheral arterial disease). Clinical concern that there is a deep-seated soft tissue or bone infection (with or without ulceration). Gangrene (with or without ulceration).

claim: NICE NG19: all other active diabetic foot problems - refer within 1 working day to the multidisciplinary foot care service or foot protection service, for triage within 1 further working day.
document: Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management (NICE guideline NG19)
quote: For all other active diabetic foot problems, refer the person within 1 working day to the multidisciplinary foot care service or foot protection service
conflicts: NICE's phrase is 'within 1 working day', NOT 'within 24 hours' (the brief's example wording). IWGDF and ADA give no hour-based timeframes - they use 'urgent'/'urgently'/'promptly'.

claim: NICE NG19: suspect acute Charcot arthropathy with redness, warmth, swelling or deformity (especially with intact skin, neuropathy or renal failure); refer within 1 working day and offer non-weight-bearing treatment meanwhile.
document: Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management (NICE guideline NG19)
quote: Suspect acute Charcot arthropathy if there is redness, warmth, swelling or deformity (in particular, when the skin is intact), especially in the presence of peripheral neuropathy or renal failure.

claim: NICE NG19 stratifies risk as low (no risk factors except callus alone), moderate (deformity or neuropathy or PAD), high (previous ulceration/amputation, renal replacement therapy, or combinations) and active foot problem; reassess annually / every 3-6 months / every 1-2 months / every 1-2 weeks.
document: Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management (NICE guideline NG19)
quote: previous ulceration or previous amputation or on renal replacement therapy or neuropathy and peripheral arterial disease together or neuropathy in combination with callus and/or deformity or peripheral arterial disease in combination with callus and/or deformity
conflicts: IWGDF 2023: previous ulcer/amputation/ESRD only count when LOPS or PAD is present; neuropathy alone = IWGDF 1 (6-12 monthly) but NICE moderate (3-6 monthly); IWGDF has four numbered categories 0-3 and no 'active' tier.

claim: IWGDF practical guidelines use 'urgent' for: deep or extensive (moderate or severe) infection - urgently evaluate for immediate surgery; and severe ischaemia by perfusion thresholds - urgent vascular imaging/revascularisation.
document: Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease (IWGDF 2023 update)
quote: Urgently evaluate for need for immediate surgical intervention to remove necrotic tissue, including infected bone, release compartment pressure and drain abscesses;

claim: ADA: perform a comprehensive foot evaluation at least annually to identify risk factors for ulcers and amputations.
document: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S261–S276; doi 10.2337/dc26-S012)
quote: Perform a comprehensive foot evaluation at least annually to identify risk factors for ulcers and amputations.

claim: ADA: the foot examination comprises skin inspection, deformity assessment, neurological assessment (10-g monofilament or Ipswich touch test plus at least one of pinprick, temperature or vibration) and vascular assessment including leg and foot pulses.
document: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S261–S276; doi 10.2337/dc26-S012)
quote: The examination should include inspection of the skin, assessment of foot deformities, neurological assessment (10-g monofilament testing or Ipswich touch test with at least one additional assessment: pinprick, temperature, or vibration), and vascular assessment, including pulses in the legs and feet.

claim: ADA: people with sensory loss, prior ulceration or amputation should have their feet inspected at every visit.
document: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S261–S276; doi 10.2337/dc26-S012)
quote: Individuals with evidence of sensory loss or prior ulceration or amputation should have their feet inspected at every visit.

claim: ADA: take a history of prior ulceration, amputation, Charcot foot, angioplasty or vascular surgery, smoking, retinopathy and renal disease, and ask about current neuropathic (pain, burning, numbness) and vascular (leg fatigue, claudication) symptoms.
document: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S261–S276; doi 10.2337/dc26-S012)
quote: Obtain a prior history of ulceration, amputation, Charcot foot, angioplasty or vascular surgery, cigarette smoking, retinopathy, and renal disease and assess current symptoms of neuropathy (e.g., pain, burning, numbness) and vascular disease (e.g., leg fatigue, claudication).

claim: ADA: interprofessional care for foot ulcers and high-risk feet (dialysis, Charcot foot, prior ulcer or amputation, PAD); refer people who smoke and have prior lower-extremity complications, LOPS, structural abnormalities or PAD to foot care specialists for lifelong surveillance.
document: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S261–S276; doi 10.2337/dc26-S012)
quote: An interprofessional approach facilitated by a podiatrist in conjunction with other appropriate team members is recommended for individuals with foot ulcers and high-risk feet (e.g., those on dialysis, those with Charcot foot, those with a history of prior ulcers or amputation, and those with PAD).

claim: ADA: give general preventive foot self-care education to all people with diabetes, including how to examine the feet daily (palpation, or visual inspection with an unbreakable mirror).
document: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S261–S276; doi 10.2337/dc26-S012)
quote: Provide general preventive foot self-care education to all people with diabetes, including those with LOPS, on appropriate ways to examine their feet (palpation or visual inspection with an unbreakable mirror) for daily surveillance of early foot problems.

claim: ADA: specialised therapeutic footwear is recommended for people at high risk of ulceration - LOPS, foot deformities, ulcers, callus formation, poor peripheral circulation or history of amputation.
document: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S261–S276; doi 10.2337/dc26-S012)
quote: The use of specialized therapeutic footwear is recommended for people with diabetes at high risk for ulceration, including those with LOPS, foot deformities, ulcers, callous formation, poor peripheral circulation, or history of amputation.

claim: ADA lists risk factors for the at-risk foot: chronic hyperglycaemia, neuropathy/LOPS, PAD, deformities, pre-ulcerative corns or calluses, prior ulcer, prior amputation, smoking, retinopathy, nephropathy (especially dialysis or post-transplant) and social determinants of health.
document: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S261–S276; doi 10.2337/dc26-S012)
section: Foot Care (narrative list of risk factors)
quote: Factors that are associated with the at-risk foot include the following: Chronic hyperglycemia; Peripheral neuropathy/LOPS; PAD; Foot deformities (bunions, hammertoes, Charcot joint, etc.); Preulcerative corns or calluses; Prior ulceration; Prior amputation; Smoking; Retinopathy; Nephropathy (particularly individuals on dialysis or posttransplant); Social determinants of health [...]

claim: Diabetic foot ulcer prevalence is reported as 7.2% across Africa and 1-4% in Uganda (Zhang et al. 2017 meta-analysis, as cited by a 2023 Ugandan multicentre study).
version: Vahwere et al., BMC Public Health 2023;23:463 citing Zhang P, et al. Ann Med 2017;49(2):106-116
document: Factors associated with severity and anatomical distribution of diabetic foot ulcer in Uganda: a multicenter cross-sectional study
quote: This prevalence varies between 3% in Oceania to 13% in North America, with a prevalence of 7.2% across Africa; in Uganda it varies from 1 to 4%

claim: In a seven-hospital Ugandan study (Nov 2021-Jan 2022, n=117 with DFU), 59.8% presented with severe ulcers (Wagner grade 3 or above), 47.9% had ulcers >5 cm and 44.4% were plantar.
document: Factors associated with severity and anatomical distribution of diabetic foot ulcer in Uganda: a multicenter cross-sectional study (Vahwere BM, et al.)
quote: A total of 117 patients with DFU were enrolled in this study between November 2021 and January 2022

claim: IWGDF: the burden of foot disease and amputation is rising fastest in middle- and lower-income countries; barefoot walking and inappropriate footwear are major causes of the foot trauma that leads to ulceration.
document: Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease (IWGDF 2023 update)
quote: The burden of foot disease and amputations is increasing at a rapid rate, and comparatively more so in middle to lower income countries.

claim: An African meta-analysis (Rigato et al. 2018) is recalled as reporting a pooled foot-ulcer prevalence of about 13% among people with diabetes (hospital-weighted), with roughly 15% of those with foot lesions undergoing major amputation and about 14% dying in hospital - NOT VERIFIED.
version: Rigato M, et al. Diabetes Res Clin Pract 2018;142:63-73 (not opened)
document: Characteristics, prevalence, and outcomes of diabetic foot ulcers in Africa. A systemic review and meta-analysis
conflicts: Zhang 2017 gives 7.2% for Africa; the higher Rigato figure is driven by in-patient series.

claim: DKA in adults is diagnosed when all three components are present: diabetes/hyperglycaemia, ketosis and metabolic acidosis.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
section: Figure 2A - The diagnosis criteria of DKA; section 'What are the diagnostic criteria of DKA and HHS?'
quote: Diabetes/hyperglycemia: Glucose ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) OR prior history of diabetes. Ketosis: β-Hydroxybutyrate concentration ≥3.0 mmol/L OR urine ketone strip 2+ or greater. Metabolic Acidosis: pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate concentration <18 mmol/L. [...] All three components must be present to make this diagnosis.
conflicts: JBDS 02 (2023) uses bicarbonate < 15.0 mmol/L and glucose > 11.0 mmol/L (A9-19). NICE NG18 (children) uses bicarbonate < 15 mmol/L (A9-28). ISPAD 2022 (children) matches the 18 mmol/L bicarbonate cut-off (A9-23).

claim: An anion gap > 12 mmol/L indicates a high anion gap metabolic acidosis consistent with DKA, but the anion gap is not recommended as a first-line diagnostic or resolution criterion.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
quote: The anion gap is calculated by subtracting the major measured anions (chloride and bicarbonate) from the major measured cation (sodium). An anion gap >12 mmol/L indicates the presence of a high anion gap metabolic acidosis consistent with DKA [...] the anion gap is not recommended as a first-line diagnostic or resolution criterion.
conflicts: JBDS 02 lists 'Anion gap above 16' as a marker of severe DKA (A9-20); the 2009 ADA statement used anion gap > 10-12 as a diagnostic criterion.

claim: The 2024 consensus lowered the hyperglycaemia criterion for DKA from > 13.9 mmol/L (250 mg/dL) to >= 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or a prior history of diabetes.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
quote: we have defined hyperglycemia as a diagnostic criterion for DKA from >250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L) to either a glucose value of ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L)
conflicts: Older ADA 2009 criteria (still in many textbooks and likely in older local protocols) require glucose > 13.9 mmol/L (250 mg/dL).

claim: The 2024 consensus grades DKA as mild, moderate or severe by beta-hydroxybutyrate, pH/bicarbonate and mental status; not all variables need to be fulfilled.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
section: Table 2 - DKA classification and suggested level of care by severity: mild, moderate, or severe
quote: Mild: β-Hydroxybutyrate 3.0–6.0 mmol/L; pH >7.25 to <7.30 or bicarbonate 15–18 mmol/L; Alert. Moderate: β-Hydroxybutyrate 3.0–6.0 mmol/L; pH 7.0–7.25, bicarbonate 10 to <15 mmol/L; Alert/drowsy. Severe: β-Hydroxybutyrate >6.0 mmol/L; pH <7.0, bicarbonate <10 mmol/L; Stupor/coma. Not all variables need to be fulfilled to be defined as either mild, moderate, or severe
conflicts: ISPAD 2022 / NICE NG18 paediatric severity uses different cut-offs: moderate pH < 7.2 or bicarbonate < 10; severe pH < 7.1 or bicarbonate < 5 (A9-24, A9-28). JBDS 02 has no 3-tier table, only a list of severity markers (bicarbonate < 5.0, pH < 7.0, ketones > 6.0).

claim: Euglycaemic DKA is DKA (ketosis plus metabolic acidosis) with plasma glucose < 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL); about 10% of DKA; listed causes are exogenous insulin, reduced food intake, pregnancy, alcohol, liver failure and SGLT2 inhibitors.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
quote: Approximately 10% of patients with DKA present with euglycemic DKA, which is defined as plasma glucose levels <200 mg/dL [11.1 mmol/L] in the presence of ketosis and metabolic acidosis. [...] can be caused by a variety of factors, including exogenous insulin injection, reduced food intake, pregnancy, or impaired gluconeogenesis due to alcohol use, liver failure, and/or SGLT2 inhibitor therapy.
conflicts: JBDS 02 (2023) describes euglycaemic DKA qualitatively ('glucose is normal, or not particularly raised') and notes DKA in pregnancy with glucose < 13.9 mmol/L.

claim: SGLT2 inhibitors account for the majority of euglycaemic DKA cases and have been found to increase DKA risk.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
quote: In recent years, the use of SGLT2 inhibitors in those with T1D and T2D has accounted for the majority of cases of euglycemic DKA

claim: HHS in adults requires severe hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolarity, absence of significant ketonaemia and absence of acidosis; two osmolality formulas are given.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
section: Figure 2B - The diagnosis criteria of HHS
quote: Plasma glucose ≥600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L). Calculated effective serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg (calculated as [2xNa+ (mmol/L) + glucose (mmol/L)]), OR total serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg [(2xNa+ (mmol/L) + glucose (mmol/L) + urea (mmol/L)]. β-Hydroxybutyrate concentration <3.0 mmol/L OR urine ketone strip less than 2+. pH ≥7.3 and bicarbonate concentration ≥15 mmol/L
conflicts: JBDS 06 (2022): glucose >= 30 mmol/L and osmolality >= 320 mOsm/kg using 2Na + glucose + urea only (A9-22). ISPAD 2022 (children): glucose > 33.3 mmol/L, EFFECTIVE osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg, venous pH > 7.25, bicarbonate > 15 (A9-27). Endotext prints glucose '> 600 mg/dL' rather than '>='.

claim: DKA and HHS overlap in more than one-third of hyperglycaemic crises, and mixed DKA/HHS carries higher mortality than either alone.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
quote: Clinical overlap between DKA and HHS has been reported in more than one-third of people with hyperglycemic crises. [...] Patients with mixed DKA/HHS have higher hospital mortality than those with HHS (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 2.7; 95% CI 1.5–4.9) or with DKA (adjusted OR 1.8; 95% CI 0.9–3.6).

claim: The commonest precipitants are infection (especially urinary tract infection and pneumonia) and insulin omission; others include new-onset diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitors, glucocorticoids, antipsychotics, immune checkpoint inhibitors, stroke, alcohol and substance use, pancreatitis, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction and trauma.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
section: Precipitating causes; Table 1 - Precipitating causes of DKA in adults by region
quote: the most frequent causes are infection, particularly urinary tract infections and pneumonia, and the omission of insulin therapy. [...] Other acute conditions that may precipitate DKA include stroke, alcohol and substance use, pancreatitis, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, and trauma.

claim: DKA is resolved when plasma ketone is < 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH is >= 7.3 or bicarbonate >= 18 mmol/L.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
section: Criteria for resolution of DKA and HHS
quote: Resolution of DKA is defined as achieving plasma ketone <0.6 mmol/L and venous pH ≥7.3 or bicarbonate ≥18 mmol/L
conflicts: JBDS 02 (2023): 'ketones less than 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH over 7.3' - bicarbonate is not a JBDS resolution criterion (A9-21).

claim: HHS is resolved when osmolality is < 300 mOsm/kg, hyperglycaemia is corrected (glucose < 250 mg/dL), urine output > 0.5 mL/kg/h and cognitive status has improved.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
section: Criteria for resolution of DKA and HHS
quote: HHS to be resolved when the measured or calculated serum osmolality falls to <300 mOsm/kg, hyperglycemia has been corrected, urine output is >0.5 mL/kg/h, cognitive status has improved, and the blood glucose is <250 mg/dL
conflicts: JBDS 06 (2022): osmolality < 300 mOsm/kg, urine output >= 0.5 ml/kg/hr, cognitive status returned to pre-morbid state and blood glucose < 15 mmol/L (A9-22).

claim: When changing from intravenous to subcutaneous insulin there must be an overlap period to prevent recurrence of hyperglycaemia or ketoacidosis; education is offered before discharge.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
quote: To prevent the recurrence of hyperglycemia or ketoacidosis during the transition period to subcutaneous insulin, it is important to allow an overlap of 1–2 h between the administration of subcutaneous insulin and the discontinuation of intravenous insulin. [...] Before discharge, all individuals admitted with DKA or HHS should be offered appropriate education

claim: Direct measurement of venous or capillary beta-hydroxybutyrate is recommended for diagnosis and monitoring; the nitroprusside reaction measures acetoacetate but not beta-hydroxybutyrate.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
quote: Assessment of ketonemia can be performed semiquantitatively by the nitroprusside reaction in urine or serum, which measures acetoacetic acid (but not β-hydroxybutyrate, the main ketoacid produced in DKA) [...] for diagnosis and monitoring of the response to therapy, we recommend direct measurement of venous or capillary β-hydroxybutyrate, which is the main ketoacid in DKA

claim: Urine ketone strips underestimate ketonaemia early in DKA and overestimate it during recovery; sulfhydryl drugs (e.g. captopril) and valproate cause false-positive nitroprusside tests.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
quote: Reliance on urine ketone testing can underestimate the severity of ketonemia early in the course of DKA because of a lag in the formation of acetoacetate, and conversely overestimate its severity later in the course of DKA when β-hydroxybutyrate is being cleared and converted into acetoacetate

claim: DKA develops over hours to a few days and HHS over days to weeks; both present with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, vomiting, dehydration and altered cognition; nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain are common in DKA and uncommon in HHS; Kussmaul breathing with fruity odour occurs in DKA.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
quote: In DKA, the time between initial symptoms and acute presentation may be hours to a few days, whereas with HHS, it may take days or weeks to develop. [...] Both conditions may present with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, vomiting, dehydration, and change in cognitive state. [...] Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain are common in DKA (>50%) but are uncommon in HHS.

claim: The consensus states that each 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) fall in glucose raises sodium by 1.6 mmol/L (the basis of the corrected-sodium calculation).
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
quote: a reduction of 100 mg/dL [5.6 mmol/L] of glucose will result in a 1.6 mmol/L rise in sodium concentration
conflicts: JBDS 06 (HHS, 2022) uses a different factor: 'a fall in blood glucose of 5.5 mmol/L will result in a 2.4 mmol/L rise in sodium'.

claim: Thresholds named in the consensus: potassium <= 3.5 mmol/L is a hold-insulin signal (insulin delayed until > 3.5 mmol/L); 5.0 mmol/L is the upper bound named for potassium replacement; < 3.5 mmol/L is present on admission in 5-10% of DKA.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
quote: insulin therapy should be delayed until the potassium level increases to >3.5 mmol/L to avoid life-threatening arrhythmias and respiratory muscle weakness [...] Low-normal or low potassium levels (<3.5 mmol/L) are present on admission in 5–10% of patients with DKA
conflicts: JBDS 02 treats admission potassium under 3.5 mmol/L as a marker of SEVERE DKA (A9-20).

claim: DKA is not confined to type 1 diabetes: over half of Black/African American and Hispanic/Latino adults presenting with unprovoked DKA at new diagnosis have type 2 diabetes.
document: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (Umpierrez GE et al.; ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS). Diabetes Care 2024;47(8):1257-1275; Diabetologia 2024;67:1455-1479
quote: Several studies have revealed that over half of Black/African American and Hispanic/Latino adults with newly diagnosed diabetes presenting with unprovoked DKA have T2D [...] Most DKA events occur in young adults aged 18–44 years (61.7%) with T1D (70.6%), while HHS events are more common among middle-aged adults 45–64 years (47.5%) with T2D (88.1%).

claim: JBDS (UK) requires all of: glucose > 11.0 mmol/L or known diabetes; blood ketones of 3.0 mmol/L or more, or significant ketonuria (2+ or more); and bicarbonate < 15.0 mmol/L and/or venous pH < 7.3.
document: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults (JBDS 02)
section: Diagnosis of DKA (p.10); single-page treatment pathway (p.9)
quote: All of these must be present to make the diagnosis: The 'D' – a blood glucose concentration of >11.0 mmol/L or known to have diabetes mellitus; The 'K' – a capillary or blood ketone concentration of >3.0 mmol/L or significant ketonuria (2+ or more on standard urine sticks); The 'A' – a bicarbonate concentration of <15.0 mmol/L and/or venous pH <7.3
conflicts: 2024 international consensus: bicarbonate < 18 mmol/L and ketones >= 3.0 mmol/L (A9-01). JBDS co-signed the consensus but its own 2023 guideline keeps bicarbonate < 15.0.

claim: JBDS lists markers any one of which may indicate severe DKA.
document: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults (JBDS 02)
quote: The presence of one or more of the following may indicate severe DKA: Blood ketones over 6.0 mmol/L; Bicarbonate level below 5.0 mmol/L; Venous/arterial pH below 7.0; Hypokalaemia on admission (under 3.5 mmol/L); GCS less than 12 or abnormal AVPU scale; Oxygen saturation below 92% on air; Systolic BP below 90 mmHg; Pulse over 100 or below 60 bpm; Anion gap above 16
conflicts: Consensus Table 2 calls bicarbonate < 10 mmol/L 'severe' (JBDS < 5.0) and has no vital-sign markers (A9-04).

claim: JBDS defines DKA resolution as ketones < 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH > 7.3.
document: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults (JBDS 02)
quote: Resolution of DKA is defined as ketones less than 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH over 7.3
conflicts: Consensus 2024 allows bicarbonate >= 18 mmol/L as an alternative to pH >= 7.3 (A9-10).

claim: JBDS defines HHS by marked hypovolaemia, osmolality of 320 mOsm/kg or more, glucose of 30 mmol/L or more, ketones not above 3.0 mmol/L, pH 7.3 or above and bicarbonate 15 mmol/L or above; it gives resolution criteria and notes mixed DKA/HHS is frequent.
document: The Management of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults (JBDS 06)
quote: measured or calculated serum osmolality usually ≥320 mOsm/kg [...] marked hyperglycaemia (≥30 mmol/L) [...] without significant hyperketonaemia (ketones ≤3.0 mmol/L) [...] without significant acidosis (pH ≥7.3 and blood or serum bicarbonate ≥15.0 mmol/L). Osmolality (mOsm/kg) = (2xNa+) + glucose + urea. [...] A mixed picture of HHS and DKA occurs relatively frequently.
conflicts: Consensus 2024: glucose >= 33.3 mmol/L and EFFECTIVE osmolality > 300 (or total > 320) (A9-07). ISPAD 2022: effective osmolality > 320 (A9-27).

claim: ISPAD defines paediatric DKA as hyperglycaemia > 11 mmol/L, venous pH < 7.3 or bicarbonate < 18 mmol/L, and ketonaemia (BOHB >= 3 mmol/L) or moderate/large ketonuria.
version: 2022 (Glaser N et al., Pediatr Diabetes 2022;23:835-856); no 2024 ISPAD DKA chapter exists
document: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (Chapter 11)
section: Biochemical criteria for the diagnosis of DKA
quote: Hyperglycemia (blood glucose >11 mmol/L [200 mg/dl]) [...] Venous pH < 7.3 or serum bicarbonate <18 mmol/L [...] Ketonemia* or ketonuria [...] blood beta-hydroxybutyrate (BOHB) concentration should be measured whenever possible. BOHB ≥3 mmol/L is a sensitive indicator of DKA [...] Urine ketones are typically ≥2+ ('moderate or large').
conflicts: NICE NG18 (UK children): bicarbonate < 15 mmol/L and BOHB 'above 3 mmol/litre' (A9-28). ISPAD 2018 used bicarbonate < 15 mmol/L.

claim: ISPAD grades paediatric DKA by the degree of acidosis.
document: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (Chapter 11)
quote: Mild: venous pH < 7.3 or serum bicarbonate <18 mmol/L. Moderate: pH < 7.2 or serum bicarbonate <10 mmol/L. Severe: pH < 7.1 or serum bicarbonate <5 mmol/L
conflicts: Adult consensus 2024 bands: mild pH > 7.25 to < 7.30; moderate 7.0-7.25; severe < 7.0 with bicarbonate < 10 (A9-04). NICE NG18 mild band uses bicarbonate < 15.

claim: ISPAD lists warning signs of DKA-related cerebral injury; it usually develops within the first 12 h of treatment, with incidence 0.5-0.9% and mortality 21-24%.
document: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (Chapter 11)
section: Cerebral injury - warning signs and symptoms
quote: Onset of headache or vomiting after beginning treatment or progressively worsening or severe headache, slowing of heart rate not related to sleep or improved intravascular volume, change in neurological status (irritability, lethargy, confusion, incontinence), specific neurological signs (e.g., cranial nerve palsies), decreased oxygen saturation.

claim: ISPAD reproduces bedside diagnostic, major and minor criteria for cerebral injury in paediatric DKA.
document: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (Chapter 11)
section: Cerebral injury - diagnostic criteria (after Muir et al.)
quote: Sustained heart rate deceleration (decrease more than 20 beats per minute) not attributable to improved intravascular volume or sleep state [...] Age-inappropriate incontinence [...] Minor Criteria: Vomiting, Headache, Lethargy or not easily arousable, Diastolic blood pressure > 90 mmHg, Age <5 years

claim: ISPAD criteria for HHS in children: glucose > 33.3 mmol/L, venous pH > 7.25 (arterial > 7.30), bicarbonate > 15 mmol/L, small ketonuria / absent to mild ketonaemia, effective osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg, with obtundation, combativeness or seizures in about half.
document: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (Chapter 11)
quote: Plasma glucose concentration > 33.3 mmol/L (600 mg/dl); Venous pH > 7.25; arterial pH > 7.30; Serum bicarbonate >15 mmol/L; Small ketonuria, absent to mild ketonemia; Effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg
conflicts: Adult consensus 2024: glucose >= 33.3, effective osmolality > 300 (total > 320), pH >= 7.3, bicarbonate >= 15 (A9-07).

claim: NICE NG18 diagnoses DKA in children with acidosis (pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15 mmol/litre) and ketonaemia (BOHB above 3 mmol/litre), graded mild/moderate/severe; children on insulin may have DKA with normal glucose.
version: NG18, Bookshelf copy last updated 11 May 2023
document: Diabetes (type 1 and type 2) in children and young people: diagnosis and management (NICE guideline NG18)
quote: acidosis (indicated by blood pH below 7.3 or plasma bicarbonate below 15 mmol/litre) [...] ketonaemia (indicated by blood beta-hydroxybutyrate above 3 mmol/litre) [...] Moderate: pH below 7.2 or bicarbonate below 10 mmol/litre [...] Severe: pH below 7.1 or bicarbonate below 5 mmol/litre [...] Children and young people taking insulin for diabetes may develop DKA with normal blood glucose levels.
conflicts: ISPAD 2022 uses bicarbonate < 18 mmol/L for diagnosis and for 'mild' (A9-23, A9-24).

claim: Diabetes UK's '4 Ts' for recognising new-onset type 1 diabetes: Toilet, Thirsty, Tired, Thinner; a child with these needs an immediate finger-prick glucose test.
document: Diabetes UK - Type 1 diabetes symptoms (the 4Ts)
section: What are the 4Ts of type 1 diabetes?
quote: Toilet: going for a wee more often, especially at night. Thirsty: being constantly thirsty and not being able to quench it. Tired: being incredibly tired and having no energy. Thinner: losing weight without trying to, or looking thinner than usual. [...] ask the doctor or nurse for a quick and simple finger prick blood test – it only takes a few seconds.

claim: A child or young person with suspected type 1 diabetes must be referred immediately (same day); confirmation of hyperglycaemia must not be delayed to another day.
version: NICE NG18 (Bookshelf copy updated 11 May 2023); ISPAD 2022 Chapter 1
document: NICE guideline NG18; ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Definition, epidemiology, and classification of diabetes in children and adolescents
quote: Refer children and young people with suspected type 1 diabetes immediately (on the same day) to a multidisciplinary paediatric diabetes team.

claim: NICE: measure capillary blood glucose in any child without known diabetes who has thirst, polyuria, weight loss or tiredness together with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hyperventilation, dehydration or reduced consciousness; if glucose is above 11 mmol/litre with DKA symptoms send immediately to hospital.
version: NG18, Bookshelf copy last updated 11 May 2023
document: Diabetes (type 1 and type 2) in children and young people: diagnosis and management (NICE guideline NG18)
section: Recognition of DKA - recs 1.4.1-1.4.2 (numbers as returned)
quote: increased thirst, polyuria, recent unexplained weight loss or excessive tiredness [...] nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hyperventilation, dehydration or reduced level of consciousness [...] Immediately send them to a hospital with acute paediatric facilities

claim: In limited-resource settings DKA may be mistaken for gastroenteritis, respiratory infection, urinary infection, malaria or parasitic infection; diabetes should be suspected in any unwell young person.
document: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Management of the child, adolescent, and young adult with diabetes in limited resource settings (Chapter 25)
quote: DKA may be mistaken for other common illnesses such as gastroenteritis, respiratory infections, urinary infections, malaria, and parasitic infections. [...] suspect diabetes in any unwell young person, especially if there is a history of weight loss, lethargy, thirst, excessive urination, ants at site of urination, abdominal pain, or persistent/ recurrent infections.

claim: In an Addis Ababa series 35.8% of children hospitalised with DKA were presenting at first diagnosis of diabetes, and the authors state DKA in sub-Saharan African children 'quite often is misdiagnosed'.
document: Atkilt HS, Turago MG, Tegegne BS. Clinical Characteristics of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Children with Newly Diagnosed Type 1 Diabetes in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia: A Cross-Sectional Study
quote: Of 395 DKA patients who were hospitalized during the five-year period, 142(35.8%) presented with DKA at first diagnosis of diabetes. [...] Many children in sub-Saharan Africa are diagnosed with diabetes only when they present with DKA, which quite often is misdiagnosed.

claim: ADA classifies hypoglycaemia as level 1 (glucose < 3.9 and >= 3.0 mmol/L), level 2 (< 3.0 mmol/L) and level 3 (severe event with altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance, irrespective of glucose level).
version: 2025 edition (Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl 1)) - the 2026 edition (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S132/S339) could not be opened (diabetesjournals.org 403; PMC reCAPTCHA; ADA slide deck exceeds fetch size limit)
document: 6. Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2025
quote: Level 1: Glucose <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) and ≥54 mg/dL (≥3.0 mmol/L). Level 2: Glucose <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L). Level 3: A severe event characterized by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance for treatment of hypoglycemia, irrespective of glucose level
conflicts: JBDS 01 (UK inpatients) treats any glucose < 4.0 mmol/L ('four is the floor'). WHO PEN training manual: hypoglycaemia < 3.9 mmol/L, with <= 2.8 mmol/L (50 mg/dl) grouped with unconscious patients. WHO malaria guideline: hypoglycaemia < 2.2 mmol/L (intervention < 3 mmol/L in children under 5). ADA Section 16 prints level 1 as '54-69 mg/dL (3.0-3.8 mmol/L)'.

claim: The International Hypoglycaemia Study Group (ADA/EASD position statement) set 3.9 mmol/L as the glucose alert value, < 3.0 mmol/L as serious clinically important hypoglycaemia, and severe hypoglycaemia as severe cognitive impairment requiring external assistance.
document: Glucose concentrations of less than 3.0 mmol/l (54 mg/dl) should be reported in clinical trials: a joint position statement of the American Diabetes Association and the European Association for the Study of Diabetes
quote: a glucose concentration <3.0 mmol/l (<54 mg/dl) is sufficiently low to indicate serious, clinically important hypoglycaemia. [...] severe hypoglycaemia, as defined by the American Diabetes Association, denotes severe cognitive impairment requiring external assistance for recovery.
conflicts: IHSG level 1 is '3.9 mmol/l or less' (<=), ADA Table 6.4 is '< 3.9 mmol/L' (<): a reading of exactly 3.9 mmol/L is an alert under IHSG but not level 1 under ADA.

claim: The Endocrine Society 2023 guideline uses the same three hypoglycaemia levels and recommends CGM, structured education and ready-to-use glucagon for people at high risk.
version: 2023 (McCall AL et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023;108(3):529-562)
document: Management of Individuals With Diabetes at High Risk for Hypoglycemia: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
quote: We recommend that a structured program of patient education over unstructured advice be used for adult and pediatric outpatients with type 1 diabetes (T1D) or type 2 diabetes (T2D) receiving insulin therapy. (1⊕⊕OO) [...] We recommend that glucagon preparations that do not have to be reconstituted [...] be used for outpatients with severe hypoglycemia. (1⊕OOO)

claim: The Endocrine Society recommends inpatient glycaemic surveillance and management programmes that use electronic health record data for inpatients at risk of hypoglycaemia.
document: Management of Individuals With Diabetes at High Risk for Hypoglycemia: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
quote: We recommend that inpatient glycemic surveillance and management programs leveraging electronic health record (EHR) data be used for inpatients at risk for hypoglycemia. (1⊕OOO)

claim: In people without diabetes, hypoglycaemia should be evaluated only when Whipple's triad is documented.
version: 2009 (Cryer PE et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2009;94(3):709-728)
document: Evaluation and Management of Adult Hypoglycemic Disorders: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
quote: symptoms, signs, or both consistent with hypoglycemia, a low plasma glucose concentration, and resolution of those symptoms or signs after the plasma glucose concentration is raised

claim: JBDS lists hypoglycaemia symptoms as autonomic (sweating, palpitations, shaking, hunger), neuroglycopenic (confusion, drowsiness, odd behaviour, speech difficulty, incoordination) and general malaise (headache, nausea).
document: The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus (JBDS 01)
quote: Autonomic: Sweating, Palpitations, Shaking, Hunger. Neuroglycopenic: Confusion, Drowsiness, Odd behaviour, Speech difficulty, Incoordination. General malaise: Headache, Nausea
conflicts: ADA 2025 Section 6 gives an ungrouped list: 'shakiness, irritability, confusion, tachycardia, sweating, and hunger'.

claim: ISPAD lists paediatric hypoglycaemia features in four groups, including behavioural signs that are often the only clue in young children.
document: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Assessment and management of hypoglycemia in children and adolescents with diabetes (Chapter 12)
section: Definitions; Table of signs and symptoms
quote: Glucose value <3.0 mmol/L (54 mg/dl) is defined as clinically important or serious hypoglycemia as neurogenic symptoms and cognitive dysfunction can occur below this level. [...] Severe hypoglycemia is defined as an event with severe cognitive impairment (including coma and convulsions) requiring assistance by another person to administer carbohydrates, glucagon, or intravenous dextrose.

claim: Impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia is a diminished or absent ability to detect hypoglycaemia; a Gold score or Clarke score of 4 or more implies it; ADA advises annual screening.
document: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Assessment and management of hypoglycemia (Chapter 12); ADA Standards of Care 2025 Section 6
section: ISPAD: Impaired awareness of hypoglycemia; ADA: recs 6.11 and narrative
quote: Impaired hypoglycemia awareness [IAH] is a syndrome in which the ability to detect hypoglycemia is diminished or absent, reported in 25% of adults with T1D. [...] score of ≥4 implies IAH

claim: JBDS: in hospital any blood glucose below 4.0 mmol/L should be treated; severe hypoglycaemia is when the person cannot self-treat and needs third-party assistance.
document: The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus (JBDS 01)
quote: During a hospital admission, any blood glucose less than 4.0mmol/L should be treated.
conflicts: ADA alert/level 1 value is < 3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL); the 0.1 mmol/L difference is a unit-rounding artefact but changes which readings fire an alert.

claim: ADA Table 6.5 lists major and other risk factors for hypoglycaemia in people on insulin, sulfonylureas or meglitinides, including social risk factors such as food insecurity and fasting.
version: 2025 edition (Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl 1)) - the 2026 edition (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S132/S339) could not be opened (diabetesjournals.org 403; PMC reCAPTCHA; ADA slide deck exceeds fetch size limit)
document: 6. Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2025
quote: Recent (within the past 3–6 months) level 2 or 3 hypoglycemia; Intensive insulin therapy; Impaired hypoglycemia awareness; End-stage kidney disease; Cognitive impairment or dementia [...] Food insecurity; Low-income status; Housing insecurity; Fasting for religious or cultural reasons; Underinsurance

claim: JBDS lists inpatient hypoglycaemia risk factors and causes, including interacting medicines (warfarin, quinine, salicylates, fibrates, sulphonamides), renal and hepatic impairment, sepsis, endocrine deficiencies, missed meals, vomiting, insulin prescription errors and steroid withdrawal.
document: The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus (JBDS 01)
section: Table 2 - Risk factors for hypoglycaemia; Table 3 - Potential causes of hypoglycaemia in hospital (pp. 26-27)
quote: Concurrent use of medicines with hypoglycaemic agents e.g. warfarin, quinine, salicylates, fibrates, sulphonamides [...] Impaired renal function (including those people requiring renal replacement therapy) [...] Severe hepatic dysfunction [...] Missed or delayed meals [...] Prolonged starvation time e.g. 'Nil by Mouth' [...] Acute discontinuation of long-term corticosteroid therapy

claim: The Endocrine Society lists causes of hypoglycaemia in an ill or medicated adult: drugs (insulin, insulin secretagogue, alcohol), critical illness (hepatic, renal or cardiac failure; sepsis including malaria; inanition), cortisol deficiency and non-islet cell tumour.
document: Evaluation and Management of Adult Hypoglycemic Disorders: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
section: Table 1 - Causes of hypoglycemia in adults
quote: Drugs (insulin, insulin secretagogue, alcohol, others); Critical illnesses (hepatic, renal, or cardiac failure; sepsis including malaria; inanition); Hormone deficiency (cortisol); Nonislet cell tumor

claim: WHO defines hypoglycaemia in severe malaria as glucose < 2.2 mmol/L, intervenes at < 3 mmol/L in children under 5, and warns that hypoglycaemia is expected and often recurrent in patients receiving quinine.
version: Guidelines for the treatment of malaria, 3rd edition, 2015 (later WHO consolidated malaria guidelines not opened)
document: Guidelines for the Treatment of Malaria. 3rd edition. Chapter 7: Treatment of severe malaria
section: 7 - Treatment of severe malaria (definitions; pregnancy; supportive care)
quote: Blood or plasma glucose < 2.2 mmol/L (< 40 mg/dL) [...] the threshold for intervention is < 3 mmol/L for children < 5 years and < 2.2 mmol/L for older children and adults [...] Hypoglycaemia should be expected, and it is often recurrent if the patient is receiving quinine.
conflicts: Diabetes standards flag hypoglycaemia at < 3.9 mmol/L (ADA) or < 4.0 mmol/L (JBDS); the malaria definition (< 2.2 mmol/L) is far lower. A diabetic on insulin or a sulfonylurea who has malaria must be flagged at the diabetes threshold.

claim: WHO PEN training material defines hypoglycaemia at plasma glucose < 3.9 mmol/L, names skipped meals, unusually intense activity and alcohol as risk factors, and does not recommend glibenclamide in people aged 60 or older.
version: WHO PEN training manual (undated; accompanies HEARTS-D 2020, WHO/UCN/NCD/20.1)
document: Training manual: WHO Package of Essential NCD Interventions (PEN) - Management of type 2 diabetes
section: Acute complications of diabetes - Hypoglycaemia; Precautions with antidiabetic drugs
quote: It is most frequently defined at plasma glucose of <3.9 mmol/l (70 mg/dl) [...] Discuss hypoglycaemia risk factors with the patient (skipping meals, physical activity more intense than usual, alcohol ingestion) [...] Glibenclamide is not recommended in people aged 60 years or older
conflicts: WHO's 2.8 mmol/L (50 mg/dl) severe band differs from ADA/IHSG level 2 (< 3.0 mmol/L, 54 mg/dl).

claim: WHO primary-care protocol: measure urine ketones when plasma glucose is >= 18 mmol/L (325 mg/dl); refer to hospital all patients with glucose >= 18 mmol/L, and urgently those with urine ketones 2+ or suspected DKA/HHS.
version: WHO PEN training manual (undated; mirrors HEARTS-D 2020, WHO/UCN/NCD/20.1)
document: Training manual: WHO Package of Essential NCD Interventions (PEN) - Management of type 2 diabetes
section: Management of hyperglycaemia in primary health care; hyperglycaemic emergencies
quote: Refer to hospital all patients with plasma glucose levels >= 18 mmol/l (325 mg/dl) [...] If plasma glucose >= 18 mmol/l (325 mg/dl) urine ketones should be measured [...] Severe hyperglycaemia- Plasma glucose >18 mmol/l (325 mg/dl) and Urine ketone 2+
conflicts: The 2024 consensus has no 18 mmol/L step: DKA can be present at any glucose in a known diabetic and from 11.1 mmol/L otherwise (A9-01). A rule that tests ketones only at >= 18 mmol/L will miss euglycaemic and moderate-glucose DKA.

claim: ISPAD sick-day rules: never completely stop insulin; monitor glucose and ketones at least every 1-2 h; maintain hydration and seek urgent advice if the child cannot drink; blood ketone monitoring is preferred over urine.
document: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Sick day management in children and adolescents with diabetes (Chapter 13)
quote: Never completely stop insulin! [...] Always monitor glucose, defined as either blood or interstitial glucose, and ketone levels at least every 1–2 h. [...] Maintain hydration and seek urgent medical advice if the child is unable to drink [...] Monitoring blood ketones is preferred over urine ketones.
conflicts: Trend UK (adults): test every 4-6 hours, or every 2 hours once blood ketones are 1.5 mmol/L or more (A9-51).

claim: ISPAD: seek urgent specialist review in an emergency setting if blood ketones stay > 1.5 mmol/L (or urine ketones large) despite extra insulin and hydration, vomiting persists beyond 2 h, glucose cannot be kept above 3.9 mmol/L, or there is fruity breath, Kussmaul breathing, severe abdominal pain, exhaustion, confusion or altered consciousness; BOHB >= 3 mmol/L signals risk of ketoacidosis.
document: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Sick day management in children and adolescents with diabetes (Chapter 13)
section: When to seek urgent specialist medical review; Table 2
quote: blood ketones remain elevated (>1.5 mmol/L) or urine ketones remain large despite extra insulin and hydration; the child or adolescent is becoming exhausted, confused, hyperventilating (Kussmaul breathing), or has severe abdominal pain; there is a change in neurologic status, mental confusion, loss of consciousness, seizures [...] vomiting persists beyond 2 h (particularly in young children)
conflicts: Trend UK (adults): contact the team at 1.6-2.9 mmol/L and get emergency help at 3 mmol/L or higher (A9-51).

claim: Trend UK type 1 sick-day leaflet: blood ketones < 0.6 mmol/L normal; 0.6-1.5 retest in 2 hours; 1.6-2.9 at risk of DKA - contact diabetes team or GP as soon as possible; 3 mmol/L or higher very high risk - get emergency help; never stop insulin.
document: Type 1 diabetes: what to do when you are ill (TREND-UK leaflet)
quote: DON'T STOP TAKING YOUR INSULIN EVEN IF YOU ARE UNABLE TO EAT [...] 1.6 to 2.9 mmol/L means you are at risk of DKA and should contact your diabetes team or GP as soon as possible [...] 3 mmol/L or higher means you have a very high risk of DKA and should get emergency help as soon as possible
conflicts: ISPAD uses > 1.5 mmol/L persisting despite extra insulin as the urgent-review trigger (A9-50). The task brief's '> 1.5 seek advice, > 3.0 urgent' matches Trend only approximately: Trend's bands are 1.6-2.9 and '3 mmol/L or higher'.

claim: Trend UK type 2 sick-day leaflet: stop metformin or an SGLT2 inhibitor immediately if vomiting or having diarrhoea (dehydration risk); people on an SGLT2 inhibitor need a ketone check.
document: Type 2 diabetes: what to do when you are ill (TREND-UK leaflet)
quote: If you are taking metformin or an SGLT2 inhibitor and you are vomiting or have diarrhoea, you should stop this medication immediately as you may be at risk of dehydration. [...] You will need a check for ketones if you take an SGLT2 inhibitor
conflicts: Diabetes Canada's SADMANS list is wider (adds sulfonylureas, ACE inhibitors, diuretics, direct renin inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs) (A9-53).

claim: Diabetes Canada's sick-day medication list (SADMANS): if ill and unable to keep hydrated, stop Sulfonylureas, ACE inhibitors, Diuretics/direct renin inhibitors, Metformin, ARBs, NSAIDs and SGLT2 inhibitors, and consult before restarting.
version: 2018 Clinical Practice Guidelines, Appendix 8 (Can J Diabetes 2018;42:S316)
document: Diabetes Canada Clinical Practice Guidelines 2018 - Appendix 8: Sick-Day Medication List
quote: If you become sick and are unable to drink enough fluid to keep hydrated, you should STOP the following medications [...] Sulfonylureas, ACE inhibitors, Diuretics, direct renin inhibitors, Metformin, ARBs, NSAIDs, SGLT2 inhibitors [...] If you have stopped taking a specific medication, be sure to consult your healthcare professional before restarting therapy.
conflicts: Never stop INSULIN (ISPAD, Trend) - SADMANS covers non-insulin medicines only and must not be read as 'stop diabetes medicines'. The brochure cites page S361; the Diabetes Canada tool page title gives S316.

claim: ADA: stressful events (illness, trauma, surgery) raise the risk of both hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia and call for more frequent glucose monitoring, ketone monitoring in ketosis-prone people and treatment re-evaluation; several antimicrobials interact with sulfonylureas.
version: 2025 edition (Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl 1)) - the 2026 edition (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1)) could not be opened (diabetesjournals.org 403; PMC reCAPTCHA; ADA slide deck exceeds fetch size limit)
document: 6. Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2025
quote: Stressful events (e.g., illness, trauma, and surgery) increase the risk for both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia

claim: ADA: hospital hyperglycaemia is glucose > 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL); an admission HbA1c >= 6.5% suggests diabetes preceded admission; insulin is started for persistent glucose >= 10.0 mmol/L; goal 7.8-10.0 mmol/L for most critically ill and 5.6-10.0 mmol/L for non-critically ill patients.
version: 2025 edition (Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl 1)) - the 2026 edition (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1)) could not be opened (diabetesjournals.org 403; PMC reCAPTCHA; ADA slide deck exceeds fetch size limit)
document: 16. Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2025
quote: Hyperglycemia in hospitalized individuals is defined as blood glucose levels >140 mg/dL (>7.8 mmol/L) [...] An admission A1C value ≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol) suggests that the onset of diabetes preceded hospitalization [...] a glycemic goal of 140–180 mg/dL (7.8–10.0 mmol/L) is recommended for most critically ill individuals
conflicts: The '140-180 mg/dL for most' shorthand is out of date: ADA 2025 rec 16.5b and the Endocrine Society 2022 guideline both give 100-180 mg/dL (5.6-10.0 mmol/L) for non-critically ill patients; 140-180 applies to the critically ill.

claim: ADA hospital section: level 1 hypoglycaemia 3.0-3.8 mmol/L, level 2 < 3.0 mmol/L, level 3 a clinical event needing assistance; any glucose < 3.9 mmol/L should trigger review of the treatment plan.
version: 2025 edition (Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl 1)) - the 2026 edition (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1)) could not be opened (diabetesjournals.org 403; PMC reCAPTCHA; ADA slide deck exceeds fetch size limit)
document: 16. Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2025
quote: Treatment plans should be reviewed and changed as necessary to prevent hypoglycemia and recurrent hypoglycemia when a blood glucose value of <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) is documented. [...] Level 1 hypoglycemia is defined as a glucose concentration of 54–69 mg/dL (3.0–3.8 mmol/L). Level 2 hypoglycemia is defined as a glucose concentration <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L)
conflicts: JBDS 01: treat any inpatient glucose < 4.0 mmol/L. ADA's own Section 6 states level 1 as '< 3.9 and >= 3.0 mmol/L' while Section 16 prints '3.0-3.8 mmol/L' - the same band expressed two ways.

claim: Stress hyperglycaemia is hyperglycaemia during acute illness that resolves by discharge; in-hospital hyperglycaemia is any glucose > 7.8 mmol/L; ADA advises outpatient follow-up within 1 month of discharge for anyone with hyperglycaemia or hypoglycaemia in hospital.
standard: other (Endocrine Society); ADA for follow-up interval
version: Endocrine Society 2012 (JCEM 2012;97(1):16-38); Endocrine Society 2022 (JCEM 2022;107(8):2101-2128); ADA 2025 Section 16
document: Management of Hyperglycemia in Hospitalized Patients in Non-Critical Care Setting: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (2012)
quote: Hyperglycemia occurs not only in patients with known diabetes but also in those with previously undiagnosed diabetes and others with 'stress hyperglycemia' that may occur during an acute illness and that resolves by the time of discharge [...] In-hospital hyperglycemia is defined as any glucose value greater than 7.8 mmol/liter (140 mg/dl)

claim: IWGDF/IDSA classifies a diabetic foot infection with two or more SIRS criteria as severe, advises considering hospitalisation for severe (and complicated moderate) infection, and urgent surgical consultation for gangrene, necrotising infection, deep abscess, compartment syndrome or severe ischaemia.
document: IWGDF/IDSA Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of foot infection in persons with diabetes (2023)
quote: Any foot infection with associated systemic manifestations (of the systemic inflammatory response syndrome [SIRS]), as manifested by ≥ 2 of the following: temperature, > 38°C or < 36°C; heart rate, > 90 beats/min; respiratory rate, >20 breaths/min, or PaCO2 < 4.3 kPa (32 mmHg); white blood cell count >12,000/mm3, or < 4,000/mL, or > 10% immature (band) forms

claim: CDC: diabetes, especially with ketoacidosis, is a risk factor for mucormycosis; rhinocerebral mucormycosis is the commonest form in people with diabetes; overall mortality is about 50%.
document: Clinical Overview of Mucormycosis (CDC)
quote: Rhinocerebral mucormycosis is the most common form in patients with diabetes and with renal transplants. [...] The overall mortality rate is approximately 50%, although early identification and treatment can lead to better outcomes.

claim: Emphysematous pyelonephritis occurs almost exclusively in people with diabetes: 96% of a 48-patient series had diabetes and overall mortality was 18.8%.
document: Huang JJ, Tseng CC. Emphysematous Pyelonephritis: Clinicoradiological Classification, Management, Prognosis, and Pathogenesis
quote: Forty-six patients (96%) had diabetes mellitus [...] The total mortality was 18.8% (9 of 48 patients).

claim: Diabetes is present in an estimated 30-75% of patients with emphysematous cholecystitis and is the most consistently reported risk factor; historical mortality is about 15-25%.
document: Menon G, Pfeifer C. Emphysematous Cholecystitis. StatPearls [Internet]
quote: Diabetes mellitus is present in an estimated 30% to 75% of patients and is the single most consistently reported risk factor [...] Historical series report mortality rates of approximately 15% to 25%, substantially higher than the mortality associated with uncomplicated acute cholecystitis.

claim: AAO-HNS: diabetes is a modifying factor in acute otitis externa; necrotising (malignant) otitis externa is an aggressive infection predominantly affecting elderly, diabetic or immunocompromised patients, with canal-floor granulation tissue and possible facial nerve palsy.
version: 2014 (Rosenfeld RM et al., Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;150(1 Suppl):S1-S24)
document: Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute Otitis Externa
section: Statement 2 - Modifying factors; necrotizing otitis externa text
quote: Clinicians should assess the patient with diffuse AOE for factors that modify management (nonintact tympanic membrane, tympanostomy tube, diabetes, immunocompromised state, prior radiotherapy). [...] an aggressive infection that predominantly affects elderly, diabetic, or immunocompromised patients.

claim: FDA warned that necrotising fasciitis of the perineum (Fournier's gangrene) has been reported with SGLT2 inhibitors; 12 cases were identified from March 2013 to May 2018; the SGLT2 inhibitor should be discontinued if it is suspected.
document: FDA warns about rare occurrences of a serious infection of the genital area with SGLT2 inhibitors for diabetes
quote: This serious rare infection, called necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum, is also referred to as Fournier's gangrene. [...] In the five years from March 2013 to May 2018, we identified 12 cases of Fournier's gangrene in patients taking an SGLT2 inhibitor. [...] Health care professionals should assess patients for Fournier's gangrene if they present with the symptoms described above.

claim: FDA (2015, label change later) warned that SGLT2 inhibitors can cause ketoacidosis with only mildly elevated glucose, and labels advise stopping them before scheduled surgery.
version: Drug Safety Communication 15 May 2015, updated 4 December 2015; label change March 2020
document: FDA Drug Safety Communication: FDA warns that SGLT2 inhibitors for diabetes may result in a serious condition of too much acid in the blood

claim: ADA Standards of Care 2026: Section 6 was retitled to include hyperglycaemic crises, added Rec 6.17 (oral glucose in first-aid kits) and expanded intercurrent-illness and outpatient DKA prevention text; Section 16 added perioperative Recs 16.14 and 16.15.
document: Summary of Revisions: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
quote: Recommendation 6.17 was added to promote inclusion of oral glucose in first aid kits for use in treating hypoglycemia in workplaces, schools, and other institutions and public settings. [...] Recommendation 16.15 was added to advise a blood glucose range 100–180 mg/dL (5.6–10.0 mmol/L) during the perioperative period.

claim: GAP: the Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023 criteria for DKA, HHS and hypoglycaemia were not retrieved and are not recorded.
document: Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023: National Guidelines for Management of Common Health Conditions
section: Endocrine and metabolic diseases - diabetic ketoacidosis / hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state / hypoglycaemia
conflicts: Unknown. UCG may still carry the older 13.9 mmol/L (250 mg/dL) DKA glucose threshold and a different hypoglycaemia cut-off; any difference from the 2024 consensus must be reconciled by the CSO because UCG is the national standard of care.
